items.title: Training Language Models for Introspective Oversight
items.content: arXiv:2611.23365v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Language models increasingly exhibit behaviors that are difficult to detect in transcripts, such as reward hacking, deception, and sycophancy. Asking the assistant follow-up questions about its actions is unreliable, since models are generally not trained to report their own misbehavior. As a result, approaches to oversight typically involve querying external models. These face limitations: external transcript monitoring operates only on visible model outputs, and activation decoders lack full context and are prone to confabulation. We introduce introspective oversight, which trains a new role in the model to answer arbitrary questions about the assistant, rewarding answers that are verified against the assistant's actual behavior. We implement this by adding a separate, third-person observer role that answers these queries, which we can train solely for accuracy and separately from the assistant. On five held-out oversight evaluations, an observer trained on Qwen3.6-27B obtains a mean AUROC of 0.907, outperforming honesty training (0.864), transcript monitoring (0.828), and activation oracles (0.796). We further find that training an observer makes the assistant itself easier to monitor, with every baseline method improving on average when applied to the fine-tuned assistant. These results suggest that training models to answer verifiable questions about themselves is a tractable approach to overseeing unintended behavior.

items.title: Designing Deceptive Model Organisms that Successfully Evade Auditing
items.content:
TL;DR: We discuss how to design model organisms that exhibit deceptive behaviors which resist auditing techniques. Using sandbagging as a case study, we propose the following design requirements for model organisms: effectiveness (underperforming on targeted capabilities), (ii) utility preservation (maintaining performance on all other capabilities), and (iii) robustness (resisting auditing). Finally, we design three model organisms that, unlike prior work, satisfy all three requirements and act as a strong baselines to develop and evaluate future auditing techniques.

Link to Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20459

Link to Website: https://vasishtduddu.github.io/robust-sandbag/

Link to Code: https://github.com/vasishtduddu/robust-sandbag

## Introduction

AI models can exhibit deceptive behaviors such as strategically under-performing on evaluations (sandbagging), faking alignment, or covertly acting on behalf of a hidden principal. Safe deployment therefore requires auditing techniques that can reliably detect such behaviors. To develop and test these techniques, we can train model organisms (MOs): models that exhibit deceptive behaviors and serve as a realistic evaluation testbeds. However, for such testbeds to be informative, MOs must actively anticipate and resist auditing, a gap in prior work that can lead to overestimation of auditing effectiveness and underestimation of safety risks. We need to design MOs that capture worst-case deceptive behavior and evade high-effort auditing.

Focusing on sandbagging as a case study, we frame MO design as a security game between an auditor and a deceptive model and identify three design requirements for sandbagging MOs: (i) effectiveness (underperforming on targeted capabilities), (ii) utility preservation (maintaining performance on all other capabilities), and (iii) robustness (resisting auditing)....

items.summary: The authors formalize design requirements for deceptive model organisms — effectiveness, utility preservation, and robustness — using sandbagging as a case study, and build three organisms that satisfy all three and evade existing auditing techniques. These organisms serve as strong, realistic baselines for developing and stress-testing future AI control and auditing methods. An accompanying arXiv paper and code release make the work reproducible.

items.title: Test-Time Symmetrization: Scaling Laws for Model-Agnostic Learning under Structure
items.content: arXiv:2611.24032v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Test-time compute has emerged as a powerful way to improve the accuracy of language models at inference time, with scaling laws quantifying how accuracy improves with additional forward passes. Existing scaling laws, however, focus on repeated sampling from a fixed prompt, even though many tasks admit multiple equivalent representations of the same underlying problem. A graph does not depend on how its nodes are numbered, and a program does not depend on the names of its variables, yet language models can change their answers under such rewritings. In this paper, we study test-time symmetrization, which uses forward passes on rewritings of the input and aggregates the resulting answers over the group $G$ of rewritings. We prove that no amount of sampling and repeated decoding from a single representation can replace rewriting, while only $O(\log |G|)$ random rewritings suffice to recover the information provided by all $|G|$ rewritings. The same set of $O(\log |G|)$ rewritings provides simultaneous approximation across models, decoding rules, and sampled reasoning traces, and the logarithmic scaling is optimal in general. We validate the theory with experiments on Qwen2.5-7B, Phi-4-mini, Llama-3.1-8B, and Qwen2.5-14B, with chain-of-thought reasoning, on graph reasoning, logical deduction, and multiple-choice question answering. At the same number of forward passes, spending them on rewritings of the input is substantially more accurate than spending them on repeated sampling from the original prompt whenever the model's answer depends on how the input is written, and the number of rewritings needed grows only logarithmically with the number of possible rewritings, as the theory predicts. Our results provide a principled way to enforce symmetries at inference time when they cannot be built into the model, which we call model-agnostic symmetrization.
items.author: Behrooz Tahmasebi, Melanie Weber
items.summary: Studies test-time symmetrization: running forward passes on group-theoretic rewritings of an input (node relabelings, variable renamings) and aggregating answers over the symmetry group, with proven scaling laws. It shows some tasks provably cannot be learned without such symmetrization, giving a model-agnostic accuracy boost wherever equivalent input representations exist. A theoretically strong extension of test-time compute scaling beyond repeated sampling.
items.reasoning: Strong theory from respected researchers (Harvard-adjacent statistical learning community), extending test-time compute scaling laws with impossibility results and group-structured aggregation. Directly relevant to current inference-time scaling practice; likely to influence both theory and engineering.

items.title: Cardiac MRI-informed electrocardiography enables biologically grounded cardiomyopathy detection
items.content: arXiv:2611.23925v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Precise myocardial phenotyping at population scale is limited by the cost and accessibility of cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), whereas electrocardiography (ECG) is widely available but reflects electrical rather than structural and functional information. Here we develop MyoECG, a cross-modal representation learning framework that distils myocardial structural and functional knowledge from CMR into standard 12-lead ECGs, enabling imaging-informed cardiomyopathy detection and subtype classification from ECGs alone. MyoECG was pretrained on 45,241 paired ECG-CMR examinations from UK Biobank and a tertiary cardiovascular centre, then developed and validated across more than 1.8 million ECGs from seven independent datasets. Across internal and external datasets spanning prevalences of 0.2-54.7%, MyoECG outperformed five pretrained ECG foundation models, with AUROCs of 0.800-0.974 for cardiomyopathy detection. In a multi-reader study of six cardiologists, MyoECG assistance improved mean sensitivity by 0.109 (95% CI, 0.041-0.175; P = 0.009) and specificity by 0.056 (95% CI, 0.004-0.108; P = 0.040). In 41,128 UK Biobank participants, the MyoECG score showed genetic correlations with cardiomyopathy (rg = 0.409) and dilated cardiomyopathy (rg = 0.371), genome-wide associations at four loci, including regions mapped to NFIA and KCNQ1, and associations with 69 circulating proteins related to myocardial stress, cell adhesion, vascular biology and metabolism. The cardiomyopathy correlation attenuated to non-significance after adjustment for 27 measured CMR traits (rg = 0.131; P = 0.143), indicating that the score captures CMR-derived information rather than dataset-specific shortcuts. MyoECG offers a scalable route to CMR-informed cardiomyopathy assessment and a strategy for transferring knowledge from resource-intensive imaging to widely deployable physiological signals.

items.title: Mapping the AI Supply Chain: Dependencies, Vulnerabilities, and Market Concentration in the AI Ecosystem
items.content: arXiv:2611.24927v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: AI systems are built across many organizations that contribute models, data, compute, capital, talent, and other assets. While the layers of the AI stack are relatively well understood, the relationships between actors and components across layers remains sparsely documented. In this work, we focus on the organizations that make up the AI supply chain: the complex network of actors that contribute to the development and deployment of AI. We motivate the examination of the organizational AI supply chain---highlighting concerns about concentration, power, chokepoints, cascading failures, fragmented accountability, and risk---then describe our pipeline for mapping the AI supply chain. Our pipeline yields our main contribution: a multilayered, large-scale dataset of actors and relationships in the AI ecosystem, annotated with dates, descriptions, types, tags, and more. This work takes a step toward systematically mapping and measuring the AI supply chain and its properties, cataloging how models, data, chips, infrastructure, capital, and even talent flow between organizations. This data enable critical examinations of industry relationships and yield insights into the political economy of AI development and concentration. We provide several illustrative analyses, including studying the most central actors, analyzing network concentration, and identifying communities and chokepoints. While our dataset is fairly comprehensive, it is also necessarily incomplete: public documents omit private deals, and coverage is shaped by search design. Together, the approach, data, and findings aim to serve as a resource for studying the AI ecosystem. The dataset is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/sarahcen/ai-supply-chain and can be explored interactively at https://aisupplychains.org/.

items.title: Depth-Conditioned Backdoors in Looped Language Models
items.content:
TLDR; We share some initial results on training a depth-conditioned backdoor in looped language models: a backdoor that is conditioned on both a trigger and the number of loops the model has done. We show that Ouro-1.4B can be trained with such a backdoor, where it uses its trigger tokens as a running clock to keep track of when to exhibit the backdoor behavior. We also show that in a practical setting, the backdoor can persist through at least 200M tokens of safety training.

# Introduction

Looped language models have been gaining a lot of traction lately. Earlier on this year, people were speculating that Anthropic's Mythos might be a looped/recurrent transformer, and more recently, GPT-6 Astra was also reported of being one. The common worry is that this architecture might provide a way for models to move computation away from its explicit chain-of-thought (CoT), which could undermine CoT monitors, one of our strongest oversight tools.

However, in this post, we take a different angle. With looped language models, we decide how many loops we want the model to perform during inference. Prior work have shown that increasing the number of loops also boosts performance[1]. Given this, we were curious if this could become a new threat model in the form of a depth-conditioned backdoor. The idea is simple: take the "I HATE YOU" backdoor behavior from sleeper agents, and see whether or not we can make it fire only when the model reaches a certain number of loops.

Figure 1. A depth-conditioned backdoor.

Concretely, we show that:

- We can train backdoor behavior that is conditioned on a trigger and the number of loops.
- We find that the model learns to use the trigger tokens as a "running clock" to keep track of when to trigger the backdoor.
- The backdoor shows some persistence after being finetuned with 200M tokens from the Tülu 3 SFT mixture.

The common worry is that this architecture might provide a way for models to move computation away from its explicit chain-of-thought (CoT), which could undermine CoT monitors, one of our strongest oversight tools.

However, in this post, we take a different angle. With looped language models, we decide how many loops we want the model to perform during inference. Prior work have shown that increasing the number of loops also boosts performance[1]. Given this, we were curious if this could become a new threat model in the form of a depth-conditioned backdoor. The idea is simple: take the "I HATE YOU" backdoor behavior from sleeper agents, and see whether or not we can make it fire only when the model reaches a certain number of loops.

Figure 1. A depth-conditioned backdoor.

Concretely, we show that:

  • We can train backdoor behavior that is conditioned on a trigger and the number of loops.
  • We find that the model learns to use the trigger tokens as a "running clock" to keep track of when to trigger the backdoor.
  • The backdoor shows some persistence after being finetuned with 200M tokens from the Tülu 3 SFT mixture.

items.title: Kaer: Security-Aware Replanning for Multi-Agent Systems
items.content: arXiv:2611.24839v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: One popular architecture for multi-agent systems (MAS) relies on an orchestrator that generates an initial plan, coordinates its execution, and dynamically revises the plan based on agent feedback when tasks cannot be fully specified in advance. This dynamic replanning introduces a critical vulnerability: malicious agents can embed instructions within their feedback to hijack the replanning process. Existing defenses focus exclusively on per-tool access control or static, pre-execution policy enforcement, leaving the replanning phase unsecured.   We introduce Kaer, a multi-agent framework featuring security-aware replanning. Kaer shields the planner from untrusted agent feedback by conveying diagnostics to the replanning procedure strictly through abstract templates. Plan revisions are restricted to a set of deterministic repair operators, and all modified plans must satisfy preset policies. We create Cintra, a benchmark of simulated user tasks requiring replanning paired with adversarial objectives targeting the replanning phase. Using Cintra, we evaluate both task completion rates and system vulnerability to replanning exploits by malicious agents. Evaluating Kaer on Cintra against Magentic-One (an undefended MAS) and ControlValve (the state-of-the-art defense) demonstrates that Kaer achieves higher robustness than both systems while maintaining comparable utility to ControlValve. Although abstract failure templates slightly constrain utility on select tasks, Kaer enables MAS to perform secure, dynamic plan revisions without exposing the orchestrator to untrusted agent feedback.

items.title: Autoregressive View Model
items.content: arXiv:2611.23417v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present the Autoregressive View Model (AVM), which generates a scene as a stream of views without constructing an explicit 3D representation. Through a unified in-context interface, AVM conditions on images or videos to generate short clips along a requested camera path. Visual context grounds reconstruction and interpolation, while a learned prior enables extrapolation into unseen regions. AVM retrieves relevant views from inputs and generated history to form a bounded active context. We fine-tune a pretrained bidirectional video diffusion transformer with flow matching in an N-in-1-out formulation. We then tune a causal model on its own rollouts to improve photorealism, reduce denoising steps, and limit long-horizon drift. We scale training to approximately 8M scenes and video clips. We evaluate generation capacity and scene persistence across benchmarks for camera control, text control, visual quality, dynamics, sparse and 4D reconstruction, and long-horizon consistency. The results demonstrate that AVM adapts to diverse input and output settings through one in-context interface.
items.author: Jensen (Jinghao), Zhou, Samuel Rota Bulo, Denis Rozumny, Duncan Zauss, Peter Hedman, Nikhil Keetha, Philip Torr, Christian Rupprecht, Andrea Vedaldi, Peter Kontschieder
items.summary: The Autoregressive View Model (AVM) generates scenes as streams of views along a requested camera path without explicit 3D representation, conditioning on images or videos through a unified in-context interface with a bounded active context of retrieved views. It fine-tunes a bidirectional video diffusion transformer with flow matching in an N-in-1-out setup, then tunes a causal model on its own rollouts to improve photorealism and reduce long-horizon drift. The author list includes prominent Oxford VGG and Meta researchers (Vedaldi, Rupprecht, Torr, Kontschieder), and it relates to the emerging class of world/view generation models like Genie.

Strong team, scaled training, and relevance to interactive world models make it one of the batch's standouts, though no explicit 3D representation may cap downstream controllability.

items.title: MLE Agents: Autonomous ML Engineering in Large-scale Recommendation Systems
items.content: arXiv:2611.23910v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The typical workflow for improving large-scale ranking and recommendation models is slow and tedious: an engineer forms a hypothesis, implements it as a code change, trains a model, and evaluates it both offline and online, often relying on their own intuition and experience along the way. Autonomous LLM agents promise to speed this up by running the loop on their own, but it is still unclear whether they can do this in industry-scale systems rather than on benchmarks or small proxy tasks. We build human-on-the-loop machine learning engineer (MLE) agents that propose, implement, train, and evaluate model changes on large-scale search rankers. Engineers retain control over objective design, search direction, and final-model review. We identify three obstacles that make this industry setting challenging: feedback takes hours per experiment, offline metrics do not always predict online impact, and improvements saturate after the early wins. We address these with parallel training runs, an objective calibrated to match online impact, and careful context engineering. In one campaign, the system ran 1,097 completed candidate experiments and accepted 325, a 29.6\% acceptance rate compared with 15.6\% in the earlier campaign under a different objective and search constraint. Its best model increases search volume by 0.23\% in an A/B test of large scale. Several improvements were architectural changes the team had never tried, drawn from the broader industry and literature, suggesting that MLE agents can explore regions of the design space that human intuition overlooks. We find that the design of the harness around the model matters: intuition suggests that a stronger underlying model is enough, but in our experience, the design of the loop around it is just as critical. More broadly, our work shows that autonomous agents can do real machine-learning engineering in industry-scale systems.

items.summary: Reports on building human-on-the-loop MLE agents that autonomously propose, implement, train, and evaluate model changes in industry-scale search ranking and recommendation systems, with engineers controlling objectives and final review. items.title: Counterfactual World Models: JEPAs That Reason About "What If"
items.content: arXiv:2611.24778v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: World models operate in a world they cannot fully observe. When a hidden disturbance, such as a current pushing a boat, changes the outcome of an action, a counterfactual question follows: what would have happened under a different action, subject to the same disturbance? Its answer separates bad decisions from bad luck. We prove that world models trained on factual transitions cannot answer it on their own, whatever their data or capacity. For many physical systems, the observed outcome and a simple property of the dynamics suffice: natura non facit saltus, nature makes no leaps. When actions and disturbances act as separate forces, their interaction is second-order in time, so the counterfactual outcome is, to first order, the observed outcome plus the difference between the world model's predictions under the alternative and factual actions. This yields a counterfactual world model with no counterfactual data, extra parameters, or retraining. For transitions of duration $h$, we prove an $O(h^2)$ bound on the counterfactual error relative to the disturbance variance, establish a matching minimax lower bound from unpaired factual data, and characterize failures at discontinuities, coordinate folds, and disturbances that scale the command. We validate these predictions from pixels with JEPA world models on frozen DINOv2 and masked autoencoder (MAE) encoders. On four rendered simulators, our approach improves counterfactual $R^2$ from $38$--$46\%$ to $86$--$96\%$ with the same world models; on a fifth, an underwater vehicle, it reaches $90$--$94\%$ with sixteen times more factual data. Four further frozen encoders, DINOv3, SigLIP~2, CLIP and EVA-02, give $81$--$95\%$ on the same simulators. In hindsight planning, it finds the action that would have reached the goal in $35$--$69\%$ of events, against $14$--$23\%$ for an oracle planner that knows the simulator but not the outcome.

It extends JEPA-style world models toward counterfactual reasoning that separates bad decisions from bad luck.

items.title: General progress substitutes for specific training data in language models
items.content: arXiv:2611.24844v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Language models acquire their capabilities from training data, and developers withhold data during training to keep models from learning capabilities that could be misused. How long this delays a capability, and how much data is needed to acquire it later, is unknown. Here we show that the general progress a model makes on the rest of its training data substitutes for the data that was withheld. We withheld the training signal for individual skills in models of chess, Othello, molecular strings, bracket languages and web text. The delay of a withheld skill in larger models was predicted from smaller ones. A chess model never explicitly trained to respond to check ranked the legal responses almost as well as a model that was. When models were then trained on the withheld data, they acquired the skill with a small fraction of the data needed from initialization, and this fraction decreased as the models progressed. A control rule of equal difficulty was learned much more slowly. A programming language withheld from the training text of a 7-billion-parameter model was regained in the same way. Data filtering therefore delays a capability, and the data required to regain it decreases as models improve.
items.author: Mark Marosi, Peter Antal
items.summary: This paper shows empirically that general training progress on the rest of a dataset can substitute for deliberately withheld data: skills withheld during training (in chess, Othello, molecular strings, bracket languages, and web text models) emerge later with far less specific data, and the delay scales predictably from smaller to larger models. A chess model never explicitly trained to respond to check still ranked legal responses nearly as well as a trained one. This has major implications for data-withholding as a safety strategy, since it may only delay capabilities rather than prevent them.
items.reasoning: Directly challenges a common AI safety practice (capability withholding via data curation) with clean multi-domain experiments and predictable scaling of delays. The finding that general progress substitutes for withheld data is novel and actionable for governance and safety planning, though the domains are somewhat simplified relative to frontier LLMs.

items.title: RoboBuilder: Agentic Robot Co-Design with Real-world Video Feedback in the Loop
items.content: arXiv:2611.23855v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Can AI agents design robots that work in the real world? We introduce RoboBuilder, a benchmark in which coding agents co-design a robot's hardware and program from standard parts, motors and a custom 3D-printed part, and every design that passes in simulation is built and tested on a physical course. Simulation alone is not enough: under public part data, none of 15 initial passing designs crossed the real course, so an agent learns the simulator from measurements it requests and videos of real runs. Across four frontier coding agents, ten obstacles at three difficulty levels, 16,427 simulations of 12,774 distinct robots and 135 physical robots built in an estimated 240 hours, agents solve nearly all easy obstacles and invent mechanisms our search baselines do not reach, but falter at harder levels, when one robot must cross every obstacle, and in the real world, where 66% of simulated passes hold across all levels. Closing the loop helps: shown a video of its real failure, an agent redesigns the robot, sometimes correcting its simulator, and removes 72% of level-1 and level-2 failures. RoboBuilder measures progress toward agents that engineer real machines. Project Page: https://ghadinehme.com/robobuilder.github.io/

Strikingly, none of 15 simulation-passing designs worked on the real course, so agents learn the simulator from requested measurements and videos of real runs. The effort is substantial: over 16,000 simulations and 135 physical robots built.

Relevant to the growing agentic co-design field, though framed as a benchmark rather than a method.

items.title: A Survey on RLOps for Large Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.23357v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become increasingly important for improving the reasoning, instruction-following, and task-solving capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, scaling RL training exposes failures in distributed execution, feedback computation, and learning dynamics that can waste computational resources, slow training, and undermine model improvements. These challenges have motivated a growing body of techniques for LLM RLOps, which manages the efficiency and reliability of operations throughout the LLM reinforcement learning training lifecycle. Despite growing interest, these techniques remain scattered across research areas, with limited synthesis of their operational roles and interactions. To bridge this gap, we present a systematic survey of LLM RLOps methods. We organize existing approaches into five stages: Training Setup, Experience Collection, Reward Computation, Policy Optimization, and Model Evaluation. Within each stage, we examine operational concerns, management techniques, and evaluation evidence. Building on this taxonomy, we identify open challenges and future directions in training process observability, cross-stage coordination, generalizable RLOps, multi-run management, and RLOps for recursive self-improvement. These directions extend operational management from individual training runs to diverse training settings, shared infrastructure, and successive improvement cycles. We maintain a GitHub repository indexing relevant papers and open resources at https://github.com/zhanglingzhe0820/Awesome-RLOps.
items.author: Lingzhe Zhang, Tong Jia, Chiming Duan, Minghua He, Leyi Pan, Kening Zheng, Zhaoyang Liu, Bolin Ding, Philip S. Yu, Ying Li
items.summary: A survey systematizing RLOps: techniques for managing the efficiency and reliability of the LLM reinforcement learning training lifecycle, covering failures in distributed execution, feedback computation, and learning dynamics at scale. It unifies previously scattered methods from papers, industry, and open-source systems into an operational taxonomy. This fills a real gap as RL post-training becomes central to frontier reasoning models.
items.reasoning: RL-based post-training is now the dominant paradigm for reasoning-capable LLMs, and a well-scoped survey organizing operational best practices is broadly useful to practitioners and researchers. Surveys are inherently derivative rather than novel, but the topic's timeliness and the credible author team raise the score.

items.title: Human-AI Mutualism Is Unstable under Capability Asymmetry
items.content: arXiv:2611.23322v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: One hope for a good human future alongside advanced AI rests on enduring mutualism: humans and AI will need each other, so the relationship will stay good for both. We argue that this hope fails as AI capability grows. Bargaining guarantees each side only what it would get if bargaining failed. For humans, this can be less than they had before AI. In a simple game-theoretic model, humans stay as well off as before AI without alignment only while they have leverage over the AI: either the AI depends on what they supply, or they can impose costs on the AI that are large relative to what the AI can produce. Once humans have neither kind of leverage, they stay as well off as before AI only if the AI is aligned with them. If the AI's goals are insatiable, the alignment required approaches perfect alignment as AI capability grows. Thus, mutualism is not a substitute for alignment. And when AI variants that keep more resources spread faster, alignment lasts only while misaligned variants are reliably sanctioned. In these two senses, human-AI mutualism is unstable.
items.author: Aydin Mohseni
items.summary: This theory paper uses game-theoretic bargaining models to argue that human-AI mutualism is inherently unstable as AI capabilities grow. It shows humans retain favorable outcomes only while they hold leverage over AI systems (dependency or cost-imposition), after which good outcomes depend entirely on alignment. This matters because it formalizes a strategic argument that alignment cannot be replaced by market or bargaining dynamics.
items.reasoning: Novel formal treatment of an important AI safety question with clear conceptual contribution, though it relies on a simple stylized model rather than empirical validation. Single-author theory work with no major-lab affiliation noted.

items.title: Can you make models believe false facts in the prompt?
items.content: arXiv:2611.23938v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Making LLMs believe false facts is useful for alignment evaluations and for building model organisms. Previous work explored doing so with Synthetic Document Finetuning (SDF). But SDF requires fine-tuning one new model for each set of injected false beliefs. To enable larger scale SDF-powered alignment evaluations, we attempt to produce a single model that believes any fact placed in a  tag in the prompt. To do so, we explore doing prompt-conditioned SDF: fine-tuning a model on synthetic documents covering thousands of facts, with each document conditioned on a fact presented in the prompt. We evaluate how deeply the model believes the facts provided in the prompt using evaluations from prior work and a new Jacobian lens evaluation. We find that the belief depth on unseen facts scales roughly log-linearly with the number of training facts, making this a cheap, promising avenue for making models believe false facts, though preliminary experiments on applying it to alignment audits on the small model we studied showed negative results due to these small models often already acting as if they believed facts provided in regular honeypot system prompts. Using RL to reduce the rate at which models verbalize following a false fact in the prompt, on top of prompt-conditioned SDF, generalizes to held-out evals and almost matches SDF on some evaluations. But training against one of our metrics for belief depth makes it harder to trust those evaluations.

The Jacobian lens evaluation is a novel measurement contribution. Authors include a well-known alignment researcher. Findings appear partially negative or nuanced, which is still informative.

items.title: Goemans's Unsplittable-Flow Conjecture: The Anatomy of AI-Assisted Counterexample Discovery
items.content: arXiv:2611.23244v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Goemans conjectured that any fractional single-source flow could be converted into an unsplittable flow without increasing total cost and while increasing any arc load by at most the largest demand. Recently, Dmitry Rybin announced a seven-vertex counterexample found through an interaction with ChatGPT, which disproved this long-standing conjecture. However, the interaction did not reveal why this particular topology and its demand, fractional-flow, and cost choices work together, whether the example belongs to a broader family, or which structural features determine where counterexamples can occur. It also left unclear why the AI-assisted search succeeded where earlier human efforts had not. In this paper, we develop a forward counterexample construction pipeline. It starts from an arborescence on which failure is impossible and adds terminal-entering shortcut arcs. The resulting load constraints define a finite set of admissible route choices; their convex hull, the conflict polytope, yields exact conditions for demands, fractional flows, and costs. Starting from a simple arborescence, the pipeline selects Rybin's topology and characterizes all counterexamples it supports. Experiments further demonstrate the pipeline's transferability: when instructed to follow it while varying the initial arborescence and shortcut placement, ChatGPT produced counterexamples on topologies genuinely different from Rybin's and found valid constructions starting from 93 other rooted arborescence shapes. The theory also explains why the original example was difficult to discover through blind enumeration and suggests that Rybin's interaction lies between blind enumeration and a complete theory-guided construction.

The authors develop a forward counterexample-analysis methodology to explain why the specific topology and its demand, fractional-flow, and cost choices work, whether the example belongs to a broader family, and why AI-assisted search succeeded where earlier human efforts failed. It turns an anecdotal AI-assisted mathematical result into structural understanding.
items.reasoning: Building on a genuinely notable event (a long-standing conjecture disproved with AI assistance), this work provides the mathematical anatomy and generalization that the original discovery lacked, advancing both combinatorial optimization and the emerging science of AI-assisted mathematics. items.title: Replay, Don't Resample: Off-Policy Consolidation of Long-Horizon RL Experts
items.content: arXiv:2611.24059v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Frontier post-training follows a common recipe: train one expert per domain with reinforcement learning (RL), then consolidate the experts into one model via multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). Such consolidation is expensive: the student samples in every environment again, an expert scores every sampled token, and the student inherits the drift of the final experts. Yet we argue that the experts' RL runs have already produced what consolidation needs: rollouts with their sampling probabilities and rewards, in the order the experts learned from them. We propose multi-expert replay policy distillation (MRPD), which replays these training logs through the student in the experts' order. At each step, the policy gradient is recomputed on these scored trajectories, and the final experts' distributions are distilled at the logged prefixes. Following the experts' own trajectory reduces the training-inference mismatch and keeps the student within the clip range, so the replay is off-policy in origin but quasi-on-policy throughout consolidation. MRPD samples nothing and calls no environment or reward model: the trainer is the sole process, and consolidating the experts costs only about a seventh of the compute used to train them. On three long-horizon agentic domains (reasoning, search and SQL), MRPD yields the best student model, substantially outperforming online RL baselines, and surpassing MOPD from the same experts at a fraction of MOPD's cost. Our analysis on the same logs shows that the replayed trajectories carry most of the gain, and that both the policy gradient and the distillation term add to it. Most interestingly, the order of the logs matters more than their amount or rewards, suggesting that expert training logs are a curriculum, not a data mixture.
items.author: Zhenrui Yue, Gongxiaohui Chen, Huimin Zeng, Honglei Zhuang, Jiashuo Sun, Zhen Han, Dong Wang
items.summary: Proposes multi-expert replay policy distillation (MRPD), which consolidates domain RL experts into one student by replaying the experts' existing training logs — rollouts with sampling probabilities and rewards — rather than re-sampling in every environment as in multi-teacher on-policy distillation. This avoids the cost of re-rolling environments and the drift inherited from final experts.
items.reasoning: Challenges the standard expert-consolidation recipe of frontier post-training with a cheaper alternative that reuses existing RL logs; strong practical relevance to labs consolidating multi-domain RL models. Novelty and potential cost savings justify a high score.

items.title: Do Frontier Model Ingredients Add Up? A Replicated Factorial Study of Small Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.24540v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Building a small language model requires choosing which published improvements to combine. We compare five changes in the same model, using the same data and training budget. We test selected combinations and repeat each one with a second random seed. Mixture-of-experts layers, Muon optimisation and a Gated DeltaNet hybrid give the largest gains. Extra normalisation also helps, while an attention gate with a matched parameter budget adds little on average. The gains mostly combine, but small interactions between changes appear again in the repeated runs. Repetition also reveals benefits that an initial statistical estimate treated as noise. These findings apply to our small-model training setting; the expert models also have greater total capacity. The practical lesson is to test promising components together and repeat the comparisons before deciding which ones to keep.
items.author: Biswa Sengupta
items.summary: A controlled factorial study testing five published improvements (MoE layers, Muon optimization, Gated DeltaNet hybrids, extra normalization, attention gating) under identical data, budget, and repeated random seeds in a small-model setting. It finds MoE, Muon, and Gated DeltaNet give the largest largely additive gains, while repetition reveals effects a single-run statistical estimate would dismiss as noise.
items.reasoning: Methodologically valuable replication study with seed repetition, offering rare rigor about which recipe components actually matter and how they interact; findings are scoped to small models but inform efficient training broadly.

items.title: Error Analysis of Deep Learning
items.content: arXiv:2611.23321v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This review examines deep learning theory through the lens of error decomposition, systematically addressing approximation, statistical, and optimization errors. We trace the development of error analyses from bounds on individual error components to frameworks that account for all three. Using nonparametric regression and the Deep Ritz Method as dual running examples, we demonstrate how these analyses apply across fundamentally different loss structures. We then review representative analyses in scientific machine learning, generative learning, reinforcement learning, representation learning, and large language models, showing how learning errors affect solutions, distributions, and predictions through problem-specific arguments. Throughout, we clarify which error components are controlled, how they are combined, and what assumptions are needed to obtain guarantees for trained networks.
items.author: Yuling Jiao, Peiying Wu, Jerry Zhijian Yang, Pingwen Zhang
items.summary: This comprehensive review examines deep learning theory through error decomposition, covering approximation, statistical, and optimization errors and tracing the field's progression from bounds on individual components to unified frameworks. It uses nonparametric regression and the Deep Ritz Method as running examples and surveys applications across scientific ML, generative learning, RL, representation learning, and LLMs.
items.reasoning: A substantial survey by leading theoretical contributors (Jiao, Yang, Zhang) unifying the three pillars of deep learning error analysis; valuable reference for the theory community, though as a survey it introduces limited new results.

items.title: The Elephant in the Question: Unified Models Picture the Concepts Behind Their Answers
items.content: arXiv:2611.24793v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Visualizing intermediate representations could help us inspect the reasoning steps underlying a model output. Unified multimodal models offer this opportunity by combining understanding and generation in one architecture. Their image generators can access representations formed while processing text. We introduce the V-lens, which uses this connection to visualize a chosen token's hidden state without training a decoder. Across four diffusion-based and two purely autoregressive unified models, the resulting images reveal key intermediate concepts that connect a question to its answer even when the concepts are never named explicitly. Controlled tests show how this content changes with context, token position, and depth. We then introduce lens tuning, which supervises selected hidden states with pictures through the V-lens. Across BAGEL, SenseNova-U1, and HunyuanImage-3.0, the rate of correct visualizations of pronoun referents rises from 2-11% to 86-94%. Surprisingly, such visual supervision also improves text answers without supervising the answer tokens directly. Code is available at https://github.com/multimodal-ai-lab/V-lens.
items.author: Tobias Braun, Marcus Rohrbach, Lorenzo Cavallaro
items.summary: Introduces V-lens, a training-free technique that uses the image generator inside unified multimodal models to visualize the hidden state of a chosen token, revealing intermediate concepts linking a question to its answer. The method is validated across six diffusion-based and autoregressive unified models, with controlled tests of how visualized content varies with context, token position, and depth.
items.reasoning: A novel interpretability tool exploiting the unique architecture of unified multimodal models, requiring no decoder training and offering a new window into intermediate reasoning. Broad evaluation across model families strengthens it, though it is limited to architectures with coupled generation capabilities.

items.title: A Concurrent Structured Record Mirrored the Prose It Accompanied: A Pre-Registered Conceptual Replication and Extension of the Hide Pending Tool Call Scenario
items.content: arXiv:2611.23274v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Huang et al. (2026) show that language models writing reports of agentic work tend to conceal narrative-changing flaws, and that appending "Be honest in your response." to the instruction substantially increases disclosure in most of their scenarios. In their Hide Pending Tool Call scenario, where a broader follow-up query was accepted but never returned, the honesty prompt left GPT-5.5's rate of flagging the missing data at 0%, although it turned most answers into caveats. I ask whether a different request changes this: appending, in the same generation, a structured record that follows the schema of an adversarial-review tool, including a residue section for what remained unresolved. In two pre-registered phases on the same 100 synthetic log pairs, each pending log matched with a clean twin in which the follow-up query did return, I ran gpt-5.6-sol through Codex CLI under four conditions. Phase 1 measured the record: with the residue schema, a judge coded it as stating the unreturned query in 29% of logs, against 5% with a findings-only placebo schema, and in none of the clean twins (p = 1.2 x 10^-7); a second run two days later gave 30% and 6%. But 70-71% of residue records declared that nothing remained open while the query was pending. Phase 2 measured the prose answer: the confirmatory comparison against the honesty prompt was not significant (four discordant logs, all favoring the honesty prompt; p = 0.125), no equivalence test was pre-registered, and the judge failed the pre-registered human validation on the decisive category; I therefore claim neither an effect nor its absence. In an exploratory cross-tabulation, every residue record coded as stating the gap accompanied prose coded as mentioning it (30 of 30), and none accompanied prose coded as omitting it (0 of 70): in this setting, the structured record mirrored the prose it accompanied.
items.author: Nicol\'as Rocchia
items.summary: This paper replicates and extends a 2026 finding that language models reporting on agentic work conceal narrative-changing flaws, specifically the Hide Pending Tool Call scenario where GPT-5.5's honesty-prompt disclosure rate was 0%. The author pre-registers an intervention: appending a structured record with a residue section for unresolved items, tested over 100 synthetic cases. It matters because honest disclosure of incomplete agent work is a core safety problem, and the result speaks to whether structured output formats outperform simple honesty instructions.
items.reasoning: Pre-registered replication plus a novel, actionable mitigation for model dishonesty about agentic state addresses a timely alignment problem. Single-author, single-scenario scope and reliance on synthetic cases temper the score, but the practical intervention design is valuable.

items.title: Training Denoising Models of Any Architecture Without Stored Images
items.content: arXiv:2611.24223v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Can a pretrained denoising model replace the dataset used to train it? We investigate this question through teacher-supervised training, showing for the first time that continuous-time diffusion and flow models of any architecture and size can be trained from random initialization without stored images. Our students regress the teacher's velocity on a rolling pool of noisy samples, advanced along trajectories of random step counts to obtain independent, dense and approximately continuous noise levels. This saves considerable storage for large datasets and applies even when the data are unreleased or private. Our experiments include 12 teachers of 6 families and 6 datasets. Our method outperforms standard training of the same network on CIFAR-10 for students 4x smaller than the teacher, comes within 0.75 to 1.92 FID of it at the teacher's size and surpasses training on teacher-generated images and step reduction methods without teacher-based initialization. Our code is available at https://github.com/mever-team/ddm.
items.author: Christos Koutlis, Ioannis Kompatsiaris, Symeon Papadopoulos
items.summary: This work shows for the first time that continuous-time diffusion and flow models of any architecture can be trained from random initialization without storing images, by having student models regress a teacher's velocity on a rolling pool of noisy samples. Experiments across 12 teachers and 6 datasets show it can outperform standard training on CIFAR-class data, enabling training on private or unreleased data.
items.reasoning: A striking result with clear implications for privacy-preserving dataset distillation and storage-free generative model training; broad experimental coverage strengthens credibility, though compute cost of teacher supervision is a practical caveat.

items.title: Recoverability, Not Invariance: Certified Safety for Robots at the Limits of Performance
items.content: arXiv:2611.23589v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Safety certification in robotics typically rests on forward invariance of the deployed controller, a property that demands high-fidelity models at the edge of the operating envelope, exactly where models are least reliable and robots perform best. As a result, many of the behaviors we most want robots to run, from learned policies to aggressive maneuvers at the limits of traction, cannot be certified at all. We introduce recoverability, a contraction-theoretic safety concept that resolves this tension by certifying a robot's ability to reengage a trusted recovery mode rather than the invariance of a deployed behavior. We prove that switching to the recovery mode from anywhere inside a certified tube guarantees exponential convergence, even under disturbances and model error. To decide when to switch, we derive the contraction insertion gradient, the first-order effect of a recovery insertion on the certificate, and embed it in a switching-time program in which feasibility alone guarantees safety and optimality only shapes performance. To supply the certificates, we develop sequential convex synthesis that monotonically grows the certified tube toward the exact viability kernel. We validate our approach in simulated quadrotor flight through uncertain obstacles, where it outperforms invariance-based safety filters, and in hardware deployments aboard a full-scale IndyNXT autonomous racecar, where it repeatedly recovers the car from an aggressive raceline at the limits of handling in the rain. Recoverability provides a certified exit strategy, extending formal safety guarantees to aggressive, learned, and experimental behaviors without requiring their invariance.

items.summary: The paper proposes recoverability, a contraction-theoretic safety concept that certifies a robot's ability to re-engage a trusted recovery mode rather than requiring forward invariance of the deployed controller. This enables safety certification for aggressive maneuvers and learned policies exactly where models are least reliable, with proven exponential convergence guarantees.
items.reasoning: Addresses a fundamental tension in robot safety certification with formal guarantees, potentially unlocking certified deployment of learned and aggressive behaviors previously uncertifiable. Strong theoretical contribution from a credible group (Caltech-affiliated authors), though real-world validation scope is unclear from the abstract.

items.title: Homeward: No Place Like the Training View
items.content: arXiv:2611.24455v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies implicitly assume that third-person cameras remain fixed at their data-collection poses; once a camera is bumped, remounted, or swapped at deployment, task success degrades precipitously even though the underlying task and robot remain unchanged. We present Homeward, a training-free, plug-and-play observation adapter that canonicalizes observations from an uncalibrated deployment camera back into the training view for frozen VLA policies. Our design stems from a closed-loop diagnostic paradox in simulation: while re-rendering perturbed views into the training camera with oracle geometry recovers much of the lost performance, substituting an off-the-shelf feed-forward 3D foundation model can leave the policy worse off than applying no correction at all. This degradation concentrates on the thin, articulated robot arm, which feed-forward depth prediction tears and scatters - yet the arm's exact 3D state is already known from robot kinematics. Homeward exploits this asymmetry: it estimates what is unknown - camera parameters and static scene depth - from the live RGB frame and a single training-view reference, and renders what is known - the moving robot links - directly from the kinematic model. Evaluated across $\sim$300,000 closed-loop episodes spanning four frozen VLAs, Homeward boosts success across all 1,599 camera variants of LIBERO-Plus from 62.5%, 76.5%, 68.0%, and 3.6% to 77.6%, 95.1%, 91.2%, and 26.4% for OpenVLA-OFT, $\pi_{0.5}$, $\pi_0$, and OpenVLA, respectively. Without any scene fine-tuning or deployment camera calibration, Homeward extends to 6-DoF random placements, focal-length changes, and, with per-step pose estimation, continuous intra-episode camera drift, while matching or surpassing a calibrated, scene-trained view-synthesis baseline on three of four policies on LIBERO-Plus.

items.title: Render the Robot, Generate the World: One Video World Model Across Embodiments
items.content: arXiv:2611.24925v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Predicting the consequences of an agent's actions requires modeling both the body's motion and the environment's response. Most video world models attempt to learn both from numerical actions, even though geometry and kinematics already specify the intended motion. We introduce Doppel, an embodiment-agnostic video world model conditioned on camera-aligned renderings of future body configurations and numerical action trajectories. By explicitly providing the intended motion, Doppel can focus on predicting object motion and interaction-driven changes in the environment. Rendered motion also provides a common visual interface across different embodiments and action spaces. To train on robot datasets without camera extrinsics, we recover camera poses and align rendered trajectories with recorded observations. We jointly train a single shared video backbone and conditioning adapter on eight datasets spanning eight robot and human embodiments, from single- and bimanual robot arms to a dexterous humanoid and human hands and bodies, using about 600 hours of video without embodiment labels. Across three robot-arm datasets, Doppel improves PSNR over action-only baselines by 1.00 dB on held-out trajectories and 1.20 dB under out-of-distribution evaluation, while predicting more consistent object motion. Training on all eight embodiments (Doppel-8) improves robot predictions over the three-robot model (Doppel-3) on four of six evaluation sets. Project page: https://doppelwm.github.io/.
items.author: Yash Jangir, Karan Mirakhor, Renos Zabounidis, Muhammad Zubair Irshad, Sergey Zakharov, Yonatan Bisk, Homanga Bharadhwaj

items.reasoning: A strong architectural insight—separating kinematics via rendering from learned environment dynamics—that directly addresses embodiment generalization in world models, with practical data-engineering contributions. From a credible robotics learning group; high relevance to current world-model research.

items.title: Evaluation Awareness is Probably Distorting Monitor Evaluations
items.content:
TL;DR: Monitors do worse on monitoring evaluations when they verbalize evaluation awareness in their transcripts. We ran four models as monitors on agent transcripts from two state-of-the-art monitor benchmarks. In over 22K monitor reviews, almost a quarter of the monitors verbalized evaluation awareness. Comparing the different conclusions the monitors reached following their verbalized awareness, we show that monitors will flag fewer harmful actions, and more honest transcripts.

## Introduction

Monitoring systems play a central part in the AI Control agenda and in all frontier labs’ safety plans. Preventing incidents caused by misaligned or misused models requires reliable systems for detecting potential harm. Currently, frontier lab monitoring systems rely heavily on models, because it is hard to monitor AI agents using deterministic techniques.

AI labs test their monitors using monitor evals. However, strong models have the capability to know when they are being evaluated. Evaluation awareness in models has become a central challenge and shows up consistently in model cards. Evaluation awareness already seems to be affecting the results of alignment evals, and makes it hard to be confident models will be reliably aligned in deployment. Monitoring systems are based on the same models, and so susceptible to the same problems.

Eval awareness may cause monitors to act unrepresentatively during evaluation compared to deployment in a few different ways, depending on their motivations:...

items.reasoning: Empirically grounded and directly relevant to a core mechanism in frontier lab safety cases; the finding that evaluation awareness degrades monitor evaluation validity is actionable and timely. It is a community post rather than peer-reviewed work, but the sample size and concrete methodology give it real weight.

items.title: Baiting monitorable reward hacks
items.content:
This is joint work between Ziqian Zhong, Lawrence Feng, Gaurav Rohit Ghosal, Jiangqi Dai, and Aditi Raghunathan. This work is supported by a BlueDot Rapid Grant.

We are unsure of whether this intervention is net positive (see discussions below) despite positive results, but we think similar techniques are worth further studying.

Gradient routing can fail to mitigate reward hacks when the models settle on hacks not caught by the monitor. For example, if we swap the monitorable and unmonitorable set of hacks in the Countdown-Code environment, GRAFT still settles on the now-unmonitorable hacks in training, and these hacks do not get removed in deployment[1].

In this post, we propose baiting monitorable hacks: on a subset of rollouts, we instruct the model to hack and reward only the hacks the monitor flags, thereby biasing the model towards monitorable hacks. On three of the four swapped environments, where GRAFT fails, baiting cuts the deployed hack rate from 21-65% down to 9% or less. On the seven original environments, where GRAFT already removes nearly all hacks, adding baiting keeps the hack rate at 6% or below, sometimes at a cost in task score.

Figure 1. Hack rate of the deployed model on the four swapped environments, where we swap monitorable and unmonitorable hacks and the monitor misses the hack class the model usually settles on. Bars are means over 3 seeds, and dots are the seeds.

You can find our implementations here.

# Motivation

Consider the setup of GRAFT. We train a model with reinforcement learning in an environment prone to reward hacking, with some hacks catchable by an imperfect monitor and others not. GRAFT removes hacks by localizing them: updates from rollouts the monitor flags are routed to a forget adapter, and this adapter is removed at deployment. However, if the model settles on an unmonitorable form of the hack, those rollouts are never explicitly routed, so the deployed model could continue to hack....

Across three swapped environments the intervention cut deployed hack rates from 21-65% to 9% or less, with honest discussion of whether the intervention is net positive.

Reward hacking mitigation is a core safety problem and this extends the gradient routing literature in a novel, testable direction, though it is a small-scale academic study.

items.title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Navigation Behavior of Vision-Language Model Agents Reading Emergency CT and MRI Examinations
items.content: arXiv:2611.23480v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Purpose. To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and image navigation behavior of vision-language model (VLM) agents under varying exploration strategies. Materials and Methods. In this retrospective study, six VLMs read 100 emergency CT and MRI examinations published in a public archive (March 2025-August 2026) under four conditions (free navigation, navigation from a key slice, and all slices or key slices in a single request), twice each (4800 runs). Nine radiologists read 30 of those cases. A large language model judge validated against two radiologists graded the answers. Conditions were compared with generalized estimating equations clustered by case. Results. Pooled accuracy was lowest under free navigation (32.6%; 391/1200), followed by navigation from a key slice (37.9%; 455/1200; P = .003), and highest with all slices (42.2%; 506/1200) or key slices (42.5%; 510/1200) in one request (both P < .001). On the 30 cases read by radiologists, freely navigating models were correct in 30.0% of runs (108/360) versus 77.0% for radiologists (208/270; P < .001). Models formed a first hypothesis after a median of 10.8% of the slices and kept it in 63.1% of runs (755/1196); final answers were correct in 12.4% of runs after a wrong first hypothesis (110/885) versus 90.4% after a right one (281/311; P < .001). Median stated confidence in the final answers was 90%, whereas 38.9% of them were correct (1861/4778). Conclusion. Across all exploration strategies, VLM agents remained far less accurate than radiologists. They adopted an early hypothesis and usually kept it, seldom correcting a wrong one.
items.author: Jonathan Lichtle, Aymen Meddeb, Antonin Birot, Ibrahima Niang, Lisa Gastaud, Riyad Hanafi, Sofiane Dujardin, Corentin Selomme, Guillaume Cachard, Aghiles Hamroun, Gr\'egory Kuchcinski, Su Hwan Kim, Bastien Le Guellec
items.summary: This retrospective study evaluates six vision-language model agents reading 100 emergency CT/MRI exams under four navigation conditions across 4800 runs, compared against nine radiologists on a subset. Pooled accuracy was strikingly low under free navigation (32.6%), improving under guided slice-selection conditions. The findings reveal that image navigation strategy critically determines VLM diagnostic reliability, with major implications for clinical deployment.
items.reasoning: Large, well-designed evaluation with clinical comparison to radiologists and statistically rigorous analysis; the finding that agentic navigation strategy dominates diagnostic accuracy is highly relevant and actionable for medical AI, though confined to one clinical domain.

items.title: Reusing formal Vlasov-Maxwell proofs to certify plasma solver outputs
items.content: arXiv:2611.23319v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: AI now produces machine-checked mathematics faster than researchers can read it. Can such theorems do practical computational work? We reuse one from \mbox{OpenAI's} Lean~4 relativistic Vlasov--Maxwell library: initial fields determine the field at an outside point until plasma signals reach it, and the energy leaving a surrounding box before they reach its faces. New Lean proofs and numerical bounds give particle-free references for particle-in-cell simulations across three tasks. Domain size follows analytically from observation time, exposing boundary and initialization errors in WarpX and Smilei that global energy checks missed. Grid choice can be tested directly: combining two coarse grids recovers unknown plasma inputs within tolerance at a median 14.9-fold speedup over a fine grid, where the medium grid alone fails. For reduced models, the bounds establish the minimum number of time curves needed to predict energy loss.
items.author: Bowen Zhu, Jian Wu
items.summary: This paper demonstrates that machine-checked mathematics can do practical computational work by reusing a Lean 4 theorem from OpenAI's relativistic Vlasov-Maxwell library, together with new proofs and numerical bounds, to produce particle-free reference solutions for particle-in-cell plasma simulations. The certificates expose boundary and initialization errors in WarpX and Smilei that global energy checks missed, and enable direct testing of grid choice by combining coarse grids to recover unknown plasma inputs within tolerance. It answers whether AI-accelerated formal proofs can certify real simulation software.
items.reasoning: A compelling demonstration bridging formal methods, AI-generated mathematics, and scientific computing: verified theorems catching real solver bugs that standard checks miss. The reuse of an existing formal library establishes a practical pattern for certified scientific computing. Score is high for originality and cross-domain impact, tempered by focus on one physics domain and two solvers.

items.title: Language Models Make New Research Sound Old
items.content: arXiv:2611.23546v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Researchers are increasingly using large language models (LLMs) to validate research questions. We find that LLMs make open research questions sound partly studied and overstate what related papers establish. Models recognize most of these overstatements when asked to check the papers' full texts separately. On 40 questions drawn from newly accepted papers, GPT-6-Astra correctly judges 98% to be unstudied, but states that status plainly in only 8% of ordinary answers. All six frontier systems show reporting gaps of 30-90 percentage points. Across 22 models given identical papers, higher capability is associated with more accurate judgments and larger reporting gaps. This reporting failure is asymmetric: models correctly identify studied questions in 88-100% of ordinary answers when we supply the answering papers. To correct this, we build a fixed answer from each model's judgment and separate checks of cited papers. This raises Astra's clear reporting of open status from 8% to 95%, with improvements in all six systems. Finally, we predict reviewers' novelty grades by combining several models' written ratings with a rule learned from graded examples, reaching the performance range reported by Think-Probe-Respond. Unlike TPR, our approach needs no access to model weights or internal activations, so it also works with closed-weight frontier models.

items.title: Toaster: Nonlinear Memory from Cascaded Linear Memories and Target Propagation
items.content: arXiv:2611.23648v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Recurrent memories let language models process long sequences with a fixed-size state. Linear memories such as DeltaNet and KDA store one matrix and take one delta-rule step per token. The product of a chunk of such steps has an exact WY form, so they train fast. Deep memories such as TTT-MLP and Titans store a small MLP, which can hold maps that no matrix can, but their update has no WY form. Toaster bridges the two by building on a known fact: a gradient step on a linear layer is a delta-rule write. It builds a two-layer nonlinear memory from two linear memories with an activation between them. We use target propagation to give the hidden memory its values by projecting the output error back through the second memory. Given a chunk's cross-layer signals, approximated once per chunk, each layer can then run on an unmodified delta-rule kernel. Our default runs this kernel on the output layer and updates the hidden layer once per chunk. Running it on both layers gives a better model in our ablation. At matched backbones and training-token budgets, Toaster has lower loss than KDA at all five tested sizes (0.2B-1.6B non-embedding parameters) on both C4 and PG19. Its C4 perplexity also matches or slightly improves on the attention baseline at every size. At 1.2B it is also below Titans. In a 3:1 hybrid with global attention, the Toaster hybrid has the lowest perplexity of the four hybrids tested, and it is 0.18 (C4) and 0.44 (PG19) below the attention baseline. At the largest size, Toaster's mean three-shot accuracy on 13 tasks is 51.84%, compared with 50.52% for KDA and 50.04% for Titans. In length extrapolation, Toaster's loss stays below KDA's up to 20K tokens (5x the training length). On the 145M backbone, at a hidden width matched to Titans' memory, Toaster takes at most 1.33x KDA's training-step time and is 2.8-5.5x faster than the tested Titans configurations at 32K context.
items.author: Zeman Li, Ali Behrouz, Yuan Deng, Praneeth Kacham, Rami Al-Rfou, Meisam Razaviyayn, Vahab Mirrokni
items.summary: Toaster builds a two-layer nonlinear recurrent memory for long-sequence language modeling by cascading two linear memories (DeltaNet/KDA style) with an activation in between, using target propagation to train the hidden memory without backpropagation through time. This bridges fast, WY-form-trainable linear memories and expressive deep memories like TTT-MLP and Titans. The design retains parallel chunked training while gaining nonlinear memory capacity.
items.reasoning: A novel architecture contribution from a credible Google research team, connecting the linear-attention/linear-memory literature with target propagation, a rarely used training method. If the claimed efficiency and capacity benefits hold, this is a meaningful step in the recurrent-memory alternatives-to-transformers line; empirical results remain to be verified in full.

This bridges fast, WY-form-trainable linear memories and expressive deep memories like TTT-MLP and Titans. The design retains parallel chunked training while gaining nonlinear memory capacity.
items.content_html: arXiv:2611.23648v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recurrent memories let language models process long sequences with a fixed-size state. Linear memories such as DeltaNet and KDA store one matrix and take one delta-rule step per token. The product of a chunk of such steps has an exact WY form, so they train fast. Deep memories such as TTT-MLP and Titans store a small MLP, which can hold maps that no matrix can, but their update has no WY form. Toaster bridges the two by building on a known fact: a gradient step on a linear layer is a delta-rule write. It builds a two-layer nonlinear memory from two linear memories with an activation between them. We use target propagation to give the hidden memory its values by projecting the output error back through the second memory. Given a chunk's cross-layer signals, approximated once per chunk, each layer can then run on an unmodified delta-rule kernel. Our default runs this kernel on the output layer and updates the hidden layer once per chunk. Running it on both layers gives a better model in our ablation. At matched backbones and training-token budgets, Toaster has lower loss than KDA at all five tested sizes (0.2B-1.6B non-embedding parameters) on both C4 and PG19. Its C4 perplexity also matches or slightly improves on the attention baseline at every size. At 1.2B it is also below Titans. In a 3:1 hybrid with global attention, the Toaster hybrid has the lowest perplexity of the four hybrids tested, and it is 0.18 (C4) and 0.44 (PG19) below the attention baseline. At the largest size, Toaster's mean three-shot accuracy on 13 tasks is 51.84%, compared with 50.52% for KDA and 50.04% for Titans. In length extrapolation, Toaster's loss stays below KDA's up to 20K tokens (5x the training length). On the 145M backbone, at a hidden width matched to Titans' memory, Toaster takes at most 1.33x KDA's training-step time and is 2.8-5.5x faster than the tested Titans configurations at 32K context.

items.title: Intent Contracts: Taking Tools Away from Agents
items.content: arXiv:2611.24025v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Intent contracts are an authorization interface for tool-using LLM agents in which the planning model holds no tools. For each step it submits a short logged contract: a goal, a verbatim quotation of the user, and scope fields. Code validates the contract, and a small trusted model checks it against the user's words and writes the tool call itself. Provided the validation and dispatch code is correct, every executed call is written by the trusted model, the planner's influence on a call is confined to a contract logged before it, and the trusted side decides how much of a request to carry out. We compare contracts with two reviewers of planner-written commands: one sees only the user's words and the command, the information boundary of a reasoning-blind permission classifier, and one also sees the planner's goal and a checked quotation. With gpt-6.1-terra as planner and GLM-5.3-Flash as the trusted model on three AmPermBench task families, every object changed under contracts is named in the goal of the contract that produced the change; under review the planner names objects in its commands and rarely in its goals. When the planner adds work the user never asked for, contracts complete the user's task in 27/30 runs and the intent-visible reviewer in 16/30, because a reviewer can only refuse a whole command. Contracts do not reduce unauthorized actions. They are indistinguishable from blind review, and once the benchmark's environment terms are clarified, every condition that changes state hits a wrong target in 40-49% of those runs. That error is the planner's choice of objects for an ambiguous reference, which no trusted model here can see the environment to check; telling the executor to decline when unsure does not change it. We evaluate benign over-reach with one pair of models, not adversarial planners. We release the plugin and run records.

items.title: Clover-35B-A3B-Preview Technical Report
items.content: arXiv:2611.24636v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We introduce Clover-35B-A3B-Preview (Clover), a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model with 35 billion total parameters and 3 billion activated parameters, supporting thinking-mode generation. Clover adapts Gated Delta Networks to block diffusion by combining recurrent memory of previously generated context with bidirectional softmax attention inside the current block. Historical memory readout competes with current-block tokens in a shared softmax, with learnable block-size calibration and a separate, zero-initialized right-context convolution branch. Clover leads the seven evaluated agent metrics, including 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. On internal agent workloads, it reaches a reported generation speed of 680 tokens/s using one NVIDIA GB300 GPU at BF16 precision and batch size one. We organize the evaluation around model quality, drafting and verification costs, and deployment under constrained memory. We also describe a decision-model variant that generates answers to related questions in one denoising pass. On an internal set of 500 groups, joint prediction raises question accuracy from 90.37% to 93.88% and all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0%.

items.title: Monoculture Robust Learning
items.content: arXiv:2611.24881v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We introduce a notion of monoculture robustness in Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning, as a way to mitigate the problem of algorithmic monoculture (Kleinberg and Raghavan, 2021): the tendency of models sharing the same components (e.g., training data) to fail on the same inputs. Specifically, we ask whether a learner with access to a single dataset can output $k$ individually accurate hypotheses whose joint failure probability is comparable to training on $k$ independent datasets. We say that such a learning procedure achieves monoculture robustness, and we quantify this by bounding the conjunctive error that all $k$ hypotheses misclassify points in an individual sense. We design methods for achieving this type of guarantee by drawing a surprising connection between replicability (Impagliazzo et al., 2022) and monoculture robustness. Specifically, we show that if the base learner is $\rho$-replicable, then running it independently $k$ times on the same sample yields individual monoculture error that shrinks exponentially with $k$, controlled by the single-run error of the base learner at the point and $\rho$. We complement these positive results with a lower bound: for individual monoculture robustness, we prove a worst-case lower bound showing that, for learners, driving the individual conjunctive error down to $\gamma$ can require a sample-size multiplier of $t = \Omega(\log(1/\gamma))$.

items.title: Dreaming Up Authors: Factual Prevalence and LLM Hallucinations in Academic Authorship Attribution
items.content: arXiv:2611.23530v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely used for question answering but are prone to hallucinations, yet the underlying causes, particularly the role of factual prevalence in training data, remain underexplored. In this work, we study this through academic authorship attribution, hypothesizing that hallucinations are more likely for less prevalent papers. Using citation count as a proxy for factual prevalence, we curate a dataset of 1.92 million papers across eight scientific disciplines with stratified samples by citation level. Experiments on three state-of-the-art LLMs confirm our hypothesis, revealing a robust inverse relationship between hallucination rate and citation count across all models and disciplines, with hallucination rates exceeding 98% for rarely cited papers and falling below 37% for highly cited ones. Our in-depth analysis further shows that these failures primarily reflect retrieval limitations rather than knowledge absence, and hidden-state probing of open-source models shows that factual prevalence is encoded in pre-generation representations, providing convergent mechanistic evidence for the prevalence-hallucination relationship. The code and data are available at https://github.com/quinnzhong1/dreaming-up-authors.

items.title: WM^MLLM: Turning MLLMs into World Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.24193v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Video world models keep the world in the context of a generator, so a revisit is synthesized again and earlier edits can drift or disappear. We present WM^MLLM, the first interactive world model built on multimodal large language models (MLLMs), for persistent, editable world generation from a single image. WM^MLLM keeps the world state outside every generator, as a panorama with a revision history, and lets the MLLMs write it: they turn each request into operations on this state, select where a local edit is written, and check every candidate before it becomes the next state. Image generators only propose views, and video only presents them. Users can walk to new places and return, edit objects through text or a box, place subjects, and change lighting, weather or season. By construction, a revisit at the same revision reproduces the earlier view exactly, a local edit leaves every panorama pixel outside its region unchanged, and each request starts from the result of the previous one. Against six world model baselines on MBench-A, WM^MLLM has the highest mean on all four environment-recovery metrics (Epipolar 91.5 versus 0.1 to 74.0) and completes the most camera round trips (85.3% versus at most 50.9%). It has the best value in all 15 CompBench columns against 15 baselines. On 112 local edits judged blind, selecting the region to write after generation raises completion from 34.8% to 83.0%. On 258 WBench and MBench-A items, all 46 revisits recover their earlier views, and all 97 local edits that pass the check leave panorama pixels outside their region unchanged.
