items.title: NarrowSpec: Draft Hidden Width Need Not Match the Target in Speculative Decoding
items.content: arXiv:2611.23835v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Speculative decoding is widely used to speed up generation in large language models (LLMs), with a small draft model proposing tokens that one forward pass of the target model verifies. Draft models that read the target's hidden states, such as DFlash and EAGLE-3, typically inherit the target's hidden width. We show that the draft's whole residual stream can run at half or a quarter of that width while largely preserving acceptance. For DFlash, which borrows the target's vocabulary projection, the trained output adapter folds into it, giving one narrower projection with logits unchanged up to floating-point rounding. We test two drafter families, DFlash and EAGLE-3, on two targets, Qwen3-8B (NVFP4) and GPT-OSS-20B (MXFP4), in SGLang on a B200 and a DGX Spark (GB10). At batch size 1 and temperature 0, narrowing the draft to half or a quarter width speeds up end-to-end decoding by 1.06-1.12x on B200 and 1.13-1.44x on GB10. The speedup holds at larger batch sizes. From batch 32 to the largest batch each GPU fits, narrowing reaches up to 1.21x on both GPUs, and no narrow draft is slower than full width.
items.author: Alagappan Valliappan, Ankit More, Dheevatsa Mudigere, Jatin Mitra
items.summary: This paper challenges the assumption that a speculative decoding draft model must share the target LLM's hidden-state width. The authors show the drafter's residual stream can run at half or a quarter of the target width while largely preserving token acceptance rates, and they show that for DFlash the trained output adapter can be folded into the target's vocabulary projection with logits unchanged up to rounding. Experiments with DFlash and EAGLE-3 drafters on Qwen3-8B (NVFP4) and GPT-OSS-20B (MXFP4) in SGLang validate the approach.
items.reasoning: The finding is a useful, practically actionable insight for inference efficiency: narrower drafters reduce memory and compute for a widely deployed speedup technique, and the algebraic folding of the adapter into the vocabulary projection is a clean contribution. However, the scope is incremental engineering on established methods (DFlash, EAGLE-3) and limited to two targets, so impact is meaningful but not field-shifting.

items.title: Rethinking Contrastive Targets in Radiology Language-Image Pretraining
items.content: arXiv:2611.24016v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: CLIP-style contrastive image-text pretraining is widely used in radiology data, where each image is paired with one report and every other report in the batch is treated as a negative. Under this recipe, two failures appear, neither of which is systematically addressed by existing contrastive learning theory: zero-shot evaluation peaks then degrades while training loss keeps decreasing, and training fails to learn from large batches. We hypothesize the cause is structural rather than radiology-specific: many unpaired reports share clinical findings with a given image, so CLIP's paired-identity target is systematically biased, not merely noisy. To test this, we construct CLEVR-Radiology, a synthetic testbed that preserves only this overlapping-fact structure and reproduces both failures. With evidence that the structure is sufficient to reproduce the failures, we develop a target-misspecification theory that explains both failures from a single deterministic gradient bias amplified by batch size, and use it to motivate a minimal compatibility-based correction, CorLIP: text is treated as positive whenever its clinical assertions agree with the image, with no architecture changes. Beyond benchmark improvements, CorLIP largely removes the post-peak degradation, makes large-batch training succeed where it previously collapsed, substantially amplifies the gains from more data, and is the only configuration that remains stable up to B=2048. The correction transfers from chest X-ray to 3D CT modalities.
items.author: Yunhe Gao, Ashwin Kumar, Jiaming Liu, Chong Wang, Maya Varma, Fuying Wang, Stefania L. Moroianu, Louisa Fay, Sergios Gatidis, Akshay S. Chaudhari, Curtis Langlotz
items.summary: The paper identifies a structural failure in CLIP-style contrastive pretraining on radiology data: because many unpaired reports share clinical findings with a given image, the paired-identity contrastive target is systematically biased rather than merely noisy, explaining observed zero-shot degradation and failure to scale with batch size. The authors build CLEVR-Radiology, a synthetic testbed isolating this overlap, and propose revised contrastive targets. The diagnosis is framed as general, not radiology-specific, with implications for any domain where texts share content across pairs.

Strong multi-institution authorship from Stanford and Stanford-affiliated clinical AI groups. Impact depends on validation of the proposed fix, but the diagnosis alone is valuable to the medical ML and multimodal learning communities.

items.title: Learning to Interact in Multi-Agent Self-Play for Controllable Autonomous Driving Scenario Generation
items.content: arXiv:2611.24876v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large-scale, multi-agent self-play trains robust driving policies effectively in simulation, but controlling these models to generate specific, safety-critical edge cases remains a key challenge. Existing goal-conditioned self-play frameworks rely primarily on static map-location goals and fail to reliably produce complex agent interactions such as aggressive tailgating or adversarial cut-offs. These agent interactions are necessary for rigorous autonomous vehicle (AV) testing. To address this, we present an extended multi-agent self-play framework that introduces agent-relative dynamic goals. By conditioning policies on this extended goal representation, our framework enables targeted, controllable scenario synthesis. We demonstrate that our approach successfully generates interactive driving behaviors that static-goal baselines cannot simulate, providing a flexible tool for long-tail scenario generation in AV testing.

items.title: Induction Head Origins of SLAM-ASR Speech Recognition Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.24721v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: What makes a small trained map from encoder states to the embedding space of a frozen language model sufficient for competitive speech recognition? The premise of the SLAM-ASR architecture is that a frozen language model possesses linguistic knowledge rich enough to perform the recognition task. This assumption, while reasonable, provides little insight into the mechanisms underlying these models. We therefore seek the concrete internal structures on which they rely. This work shows that SLAM-ASR models rely on induction heads of the frozen language model: the same heads that copy repeated token sequences in text are also important for mapping speech embeddings to transcript tokens. Moreover, we find pairs of heads that behave as a constrained form of differential attention, cancelling attention noise and sharpening attention onto the previously generated word. Finally, we show how induction heads could be used to improve transcription quality under noisy audio.

items.title: Can Programs Replace LLM Judges? Executable Program Judges for Scalable and Efficient Relevance Labeling
items.content: arXiv:2611.24849v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large language model (LLM) judges have become a common way to create large-scale relevance judgments for retrieval evaluation. However, each judgment requires a potentially expensive call to a frontier model, and the judgments are hard to interpret and may not be reproducible. In this paper, we ask whether an LLM can write a readable program for each topic that replaces its per-document judgments. To address these issues, we propose ExecJudges, a method for generating fast, inspectable and scalable judges for automatic relevance labeling. Specifically, ExecJudges uses a frontier LLM to turn assessment guidelines into executable programs, which rely only on lexical matching, standard NLP libraries like parsers, and pool statistics. An ExecJudges-L variant also uses examples of human labels if available. We evaluate ExecJudges on seven TREC collections by comparing the produced labels with trained NIST assessors, frontier LLM judges, and recently proposed per-topic classifiers. Our results show that ExecJudges agrees with NIST assessors at the level of the Claude Sonnet 5.5 LLM judges on TREC DL 2019-2021. With a small number of human labels per topic, the ExecJudges-L variant agrees with NIST more than per-topic classifiers with the same labels on all seven collections, and either exceeds the agreement of LLM judges provided the same labels or is within about 0.05 of it in Krippendorff's alpha. The labels rank the official TREC DL runs with Kendall's tau of 0.87 to 0.94, and writing the programs incurs a one-time cost of $0.17 to $0.49 per topic, with no additional costs for grading. Our results suggest that ExecJudges offers a reproducible, inspectable, efficient and cost-effective alternative to LLM judges for labeling deep result pools for system evaluation or ranking improvements.

items.title: When accuracy hides risk: risk-controlled confirmation of the critical view of safety under expert disagreement
items.content: arXiv:2611.23781v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Automated assessment of the critical view of safety (CVS) in laparoscopic cholecystectomy has advanced rapidly, but a deployed check must decide, before the first clip, whether to confirm CVS. The standard rule calibrates a threshold so that false confirmations are rare on average. We show that this rule concentrates its errors on disputed videos, which one of three expert raters judged sufficient, and that the failure is structural. When reference labels are votes of a panel sampled from a larger expert pool, the rule that maximizes sensitivity at a fixed average false-confirmation rate also maximizes false confirmation of disputed videos, and for recognizers that recover expert judgement with less noise this rate rises with accuracy. We propose certified confirmation, a risk-controlled monitoring rule whose threshold is selected by multiple testing so that, with probability at least 1 - {\delta}, false confirmation is at most {\alpha} overall, among disputed videos, within vendor and country groups, and before CVS is visible, using disputed labels only to calibrate. In a pre-specified, hash-locked evaluation on the 300 test videos (18 countries) of the SAGES CVS Challenge, standard calibration falsely confirmed 8 of 39 disputed videos (0.21; one-sided p = 0.037 against {\alpha} = 0.10), whereas certified confirmation confirmed 2 (one-sided 95% upper bound 0.15). On development data, protection held for vendor and country groups left out of calibration. The cost was confirming 10% rather than 35% of sufficient videos on time. Average accuracy hides this risk; disputed cases must be protected explicitly.

It is an important contribution on deploying safety-critical medical AI under label ambiguity.

items.title: TRoPE: Topology-aware Relative Positional Encoding for 4D Generation
items.content: arXiv:2611.23933v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Video-to-4D mesh generation has made substantial progress in recovering dynamic 3D geometry and motion from monocular videos. However, commonly used feed-forward approaches remain prone to sticking artifacts, where geodesically distant vertices move together incorrectly when they become spatially close. We attribute this failure to cross-part motion leakage: spatially nearby yet structurally distant vertices may retrieve similar motion information when motion decoding fails to distinguish spatial proximity from mesh connectivity. To address this issue, we introduce TRoPE, a topology-aware relative positional encoding that makes mesh connectivity explicit in the interaction between vertex queries and mesh-supported motion sources. TRoPE derives spectral features from the graph Laplacian and constructs pairwise topological relations from distances between multi-scale diffusion features, using these relations to modulate vertex--anchor attention through rotary phases. We further introduce a vertex-wise tail-risk objective that emphasizes persistently high-error vertices to explicitly suppress sticking artifacts. To better characterize and quantify these failures, we introduce MeshSticking-4D, a dedicated benchmark for this failure mode. Experiments on MeshSticking-4D show that TRoPE suppresses sticking artifacts while improving overall motion accuracy. Compared with the baseline, it reduces the worst-vertex error by 39.4% and lowers the separation failure rate from 49.35% to 34.90%. Additional evaluations on Motion-80 and Motion324-Subset show lower tail errors on diverse objects, while transfer to Mesh4D demonstrates applicability across backbones.

items.title: SCOPE: Single-Cell Omics Prediction from Histology via RNA-Protein Prior Enhancement
items.content: arXiv:2611.24104v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Predicting the RNA and protein content of cells from routine H&E images could extend spatial molecular profiling to existing slide archives. However, both H&E-spatial proteomics and H&E-spatial transcriptomics paired datasets are limited by the number of available markers and the insufficient availability of high-quality, cell-resolved data. We present SCOPE (Single-Cell Omics Prediction via RNA-protein prior Enhancement), a unified framework that leverages biologically complementary information between RNA and proteins to address the limited availability of single-omics supervision. Our key insight is that, although RNA and proteins represent distinct molecular modalities, their biological relationships provide valuable shared knowledge that can benefit single-omics prediction tasks. To this end, SCOPE introduces biologically informed biomarker priors to enhance shared gene-level representations, enabling knowledge transfer across RNA and protein modalities through gene-protein correspondence and molecular associations. By exploiting these complementary relationships, SCOPE enables both prediction tasks to benefit from a shared backbone enriched with cross-omics biological knowledge. Furthermore, its biomarker correlation design facilitates the prediction of unseen markers, extending spatially resolved molecular profiling beyond directly supervised targets. Across test datasets spanning 16 organs, SCOPE improves the average RNA Pearson correlation over the strongest baseline by 8.8%. On two external protein cohorts, it improves the average Pearson correlation over the strongest baseline by 9.7% for seen markers and 11.9% for unseen markers.

items.title: PhysResponse: Probing the Physics of Video Generation with Controlled Interventions
items.content: arXiv:2611.24419v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Video generation models are increasingly viewed as world simulators, which requires not only plausible motion but dynamics that respond correctly to specified physical parameters. Existing models, datasets and benchmarks, however, largely target physical plausibility, leaving this physical parameter responsiveness insufficiently explored. We introduce PhysResponse, a benchmark that measures it at two levels: scene-conditioned simulator inversion recovers the effective gravity, friction and initial speed of generated motion, and event evaluation tests outcomes near and across critical transitions. Evaluating ten image-to-video models, we find that even the lowest parameter errors exceed those of physically correct videos by over an order of magnitude, that models rarely reproduce both outcomes of a transition pair, and that the two levels expose complementary failures that visual metrics such as PSNR miss. To supply the missing training signal, we construct 72,000 simulated videos of 20 multi-object interaction types with controlled parameters; fine-tuning on them lowers parameter errors, even on held-out interaction types, and transfers to real videos and an external physics benchmark. Continued training with a numerical encoder further lowers all three errors on held-out types. PhysResponse provides a foundation for world simulators that follow physical conditions, not just appearances.

items.title: $Z$-sight: Unifying Vision-Language-Action and Latent World Modeling
items.content: arXiv:2611.24940v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We introduce $Z$-sight, a unified robot foundation model that couples vision-language-action (VLA) and generative latent world modeling. Video-based world action models (WAMs) show the value of joint future-and-action generation for control, yet inherit the heavy cost of video generators. Recent latent-space policies avoid pixel generation, yet typically align intermediate features or rely on frozen target encoders, decoupling future prediction from the VLM's native feature space. $Z$-sight instead predicts the future directly in the visual token space in which its VLM perceives the present. Coupling a foresight expert and a continuous action expert with the VLM in a mixture-of-transformers, $Z$-sight jointly denoises future spatial tokens and actions at inference without pixel reconstruction or external encoders. Trained on human video and robot trajectories, $Z$-sight achieves 81.9% success on SIMPLE (+9.6 points over the strongest baseline) and 73.3% across six Unitree G1 tasks (+20.0 points) at 110 ms per chunk, while remaining competitive on tabletop benchmarks.

items.title: ExecGap: Exploiting Command-Execution Gap for Patch Attacks on Vision-Language-Action Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.23714v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation and show strong promise for real-world deployment, making adversarial robustness critical for reliable robot operation. Existing adversarial attacks on VLA-controlled robots mainly optimize prediction-level discrepancies or rollout-level deviations to disrupt manipulation. However, they rarely account for the fact that VLA-predicted commands are not executed directly, but must be realized through downstream control and robot embodiment. In this paper, we propose ExecGap, an adversarial patch attack framework that exploits this command-execution gap to expose embodiment-specific execution vulnerabilities. Specifically, ExecGap biases VLA-predicted task-space commands toward low-executability directions, which are estimated from kinematic inefficiency and dynamic weak actuation. This induces execution degradation, where the predicted command becomes difficult to realize effectively, thereby impairing task completion. Extensive simulation experiments across multiple VLA policies show that ExecGap induces larger command-execution mismatch and weaker realized execution than existing patch attacks. Real-robot experiments further validate that the deployed patch can induce execution degradation on physical platforms.
items.author: Keke Tang, Guolin Qiu, Tianyu Hao, Daizong Liu, Yikai Zhang, Peican Zhu, Zhihong Tian
items.summary: This paper introduces ExecGap, an adversarial patch attack framework targeting vision-language-action (VLA) models used in robotic manipulation. Unlike prior attacks that disrupt predictions or rollouts directly, ExecGap exploits the gap between a VLA's predicted commands and their actual execution through downstream control stacks and robot embodiment, revealing embodiment-specific vulnerabilities. This matters because VLA robots are moving toward real-world deployment, and robustness testing at the execution level exposes a previously underexamined attack surface.
items.reasoning: The work addresses a genuinely novel angle in VLA adversarial robustness by modeling the command-execution gap rather than prediction-level discrepancies, which is relevant as embodied AI systems approach deployment. It is security-oriented research that could inform defenses, but it is an incremental attack framework from academic authors rather than a major lab release, and the abstract does not indicate broad evaluation across many embodiments, tempering its immediate impact.

items.title: ProbeShare: Probing a Few, Sharing Across Many for Fast World-Model Planning
items.content: arXiv:2611.24229v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Visual planning with a frozen joint-embedding world model supports robotic reaching and object manipulation by evaluating candidate action sequences against an image goal before execution. Standard cross-entropy method (CEM) planners roll out every candidate independently through a billion-parameter predictor, even when nearby actions induce similar scene changes. This redundant computation grows with population size and search rounds, slowing closed-loop replanning. We observe that candidates within a planning step share an observation history and thus a common action-to-feature map. Based on this insight, we propose ProbeShare, which measures local responses with a few representative probes and reconstructs each candidate's feature grid through scene-conditioned, geometry-aware weighting. When promising candidates move beyond existing probe coverage, ProbeShare evaluates a new probe to rescore nearby candidates. items.title: HINT-WAM: Hindsight-Informed Training for World Action Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.24789v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: World action models (WAMs) have shown promising generalization and data efficiency in robot manipulation by coupling action generation with predictions of future visual dynamics. Translating these capabilities into reliable task execution, however, remains a challenge for existing post-training methods. Offline supervised fine-tuning provides dense supervision on expert trajectories, but its flow-matching action expert is trained only on noised demonstration actions and never on the intermediate states produced by its own sampler; task-specific adaptation can also compromise pretrained capabilities. On-policy reinforcement learning trains on the policy's own behavior, yet sparse task rewards make exploration and credit assignment difficult, while dense reward shaping still provides scalar evaluations rather than direct action targets. We introduce \textbf{HINT-WAM}, the first on-policy self-distillation framework that supervises the action expert on its own sampling trajectories using hindsight, the future video of the demonstration, as privileged information available to the WAM itself. For each demonstration observation, the student generates its action through its own denoising trajectory, and at the states along this trajectory the same model acts as a teacher conditioned additionally on this hindsight, providing a conditional action distribution as a dense training target, while the student sees only deployment-time inputs and needs no environmental rewards or simulator interaction. To transfer this supervision to a flow-matching action expert, HINT-WAM distills the teacher into the student with an energy score, a distribution-level objective that matches the teacher's action distribution from the student's own samples rather than regressing its velocity field. The project web is available in https://tuandattt.github.io/hintwam/.
items.author: Phuong Tuan Dat, Qi Li, Xinchao Wang
items.summary: HINT-WAM addresses the gap between generalization and reliable execution in world action models for robot manipulation, noting that offline fine-tuning never trains on the model's own intermediate sampled states while on-policy RL suffers from sparse rewards. The hindsight-informed training approach relabels outcomes to provide denser supervision grounded in the policy's own behavior, improving reliable task execution while preserving pretrained capabilities.
items.reasoning: Targets a genuine and timely weakness in post-training world action models, with a principled training contribution bridging imitation and RL. Novelty is good, though results would need strong empirical validation to reach top-tier importance.

items.title: GPT-6.2 Astra scores below chance on TASTE; GPT-6 Astra and Fable 5.2 near chance
items.content:
TASTE was released in Aug 2026, and it aims to evaluate models’ capacity for research taste. Specifically, it measures how much models agree with human researchers when choosing the better of two synthetically generated safety research proposals. [1]

In light of recent evidence of AI uplift for AI R&D, I ran this benchmark on newly released models. Astra 6.2 agrees with researchers significantly less often than chance. Neither Astra 6 nor Fable 5.2 performs significantly different from chance.

Note: I wrote most of this before seeing this post, which highlights some limitations of TASTE. In particular, on proposal pairs that mention mech-interp, picking the proposal with fewer mech-interp terms beats expert agreement [2]; on non-interp pairs, performance is negatively correlated with stronger models (by ECI).

An example research proposal, Figure 3 from TASTE.

Figure 1 from TASTE, with Astra 6.2, Astra 6, and Fable 5.2 added. Results from previous models are copied directly.

Specifically, Astra 6.2 agrees with gold labels (ratings determined by a group of researchers after deliberation) 35% of the time. Its stated probability of agreeing with the gold label is more bimodal than the other two models, leaning against the gold label. [3]

Meanwhile, Astra 6 agrees with gold labels on 41% of the pairs, and Fable 5.2 on 53%. Since there are 92 pairs, random guessing would reasonably result in 40% to 60% accuracy, and both models fall within this range. [4]

The original authors mention how Fable 5 performed well (69% accuracy) in a particular category where the proposals come from different generating prompts:

While there is currently a noticeable gap versus human performance, we think future models could close it: Fable 5 achieves 69% accuracy on 74 pairs of proposals drawn from different prompts, and we find some evidence that models over-focus on how well proposals answer the motivating question when shown on pairs from the same prompt....

The post situates results against prior work highlighting TASTE limitations, such as mech-interp term-count artifacts and negative correlation of performance with model strength on non-interp pairs.

Timely and relevant to safety-capability forecasting, though it inherits TASTE's known validity problems and is a single-benchmark study.

items.title: Screening schemers: Mechanism Design for Deceptive Alignment
items.content:
Thanks to Piotr Dworczak, Annie Liang, and Alessandro Pavan for helpful discussions.

Various Anthropic and OpenAI models provided research assistance. The text is primarily human-written with short passages written by AI and grammar and clarity checks by AI. Proofs are in a separate appendix. All errors are my responsibility.

# 1. Introduction

Current AI systems often think explicitly about whether they are being monitored, tested, or trained and often behave differently when they believe this to be the case (Greenblatt et al. 2024; Meinke et al. 2024). A prominent concern is that a strategically sophisticated and situationally aware AI may conceal goals during training to avoid changes it would otherwise undergo. This is a form of deceptive alignment. This note uses screening techniques from mechanism design to ask what kinds of training and deployment rules incentivise honest training behaviour and which of these best balance alignment with the benefits of deployment.

We consider a game between a designer and an AI. The AI has preferences over its deployed behaviour that are unknown to the designer. We call the AI's initial preference over deployment behaviour its type. The designer chooses and commits to a training rule and deployment rule, which together constitute a mechanism. Training shifts the AI's preferences over deployed behaviour, depending on its training behaviour. The AI anticipates these changes and dislikes departures from its original preferences. The deployment rule specifies the degree of deployment and can also depend on the AI's training behaviour. The designer likes alignment—AI preferences close to the designer's own preferences—but also bears a cost from forgoing deployment. We say that a mechanism is incentive compatible if it is optimal for the AI to act in accordance with its true type during training....
items.author: AidanGoth
items.summary: Applies screening techniques from economic mechanism design to deceptive alignment, modeling a game between a designer and an AI whose deployment-behavior preferences (type) are unknown to the designer. The work derives which training and deployment rules incentivize honest training behavior and which best balance alignment costs against deployment benefits, with formal proofs in an appendix.
items.reasoning: A rigorous, original theoretical contribution importing mature mechanism-design machinery into alignment research, grounded in empirical findings on situational awareness (Greenblatt, Meinke et al.). Formal game-theoretic treatment of deceptive alignment is rare and valuable, though the model's assumptions about AI types and designer payoffs require scrutiny.

items.title: Mathematical proof, powered by AI. And no hallucinations!
items.content: Every day brings new evidence of the awesome power of AI. There have been dramatic developments in mathematics: AI models are solving tough problems from Mathematical Olympiads and even some big open research problems. But AI agents are notorious for simply making stuff up, or “hallucinating”: don’t we have to check their solutions carefully? In fact, the computer can check the agent’s proofs for us, and better still, proof checking can be interleaved with proof generation, keeping it on the right track. To be checked, the proof must be written in some logical formalism: a precise language that expresses mathematical reasoning. Proof assistants are apps designed for writing and checking formal proofs. They include Lean, favored by many mathematicians; HOL Light, used at AWS to formally verify high-performance cryptographic code (including for post-quantum cryptography); and Isabelle, used at AWS to verify the Nitro Isolation Engine. They were originally built to help human users write proofs, but now the “user” will be an AI agent. Most proof assistants are suitable for this task. In this post, we’ll focus on Isabelle. To generate formal proofs, we need a way for the AI agent and the proof assistant to talk to each other. Fortunately, we have the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which is supported by all the leading AI agents. Conceptually, the MCP is a wire connecting an agent to a tool (here, a proof assistant), which may need to be modified to accept the connection. Some proof assistants, like HOL Light, provide a simple command-line interface, sometimes called a REPL (for read-eval-print loop): the user types commands, and HOL Light replies. Connecting an agent to a REPL is easy. But most proof assistants provide sophisticated user interfaces, such as the Lean extension for Microsoft VS Code. That’s great for human users, but an AI agent needs something simple and direct. So we are proud to announce the following tools, which are publicly available in the AutoCorrode verification suite: I/Q: This enables an AI agent to communicate with a live Isabelle session running on your computers. It allows you to temporarily hand over control of the proof assistant to the AI to fill in some formal material or to assess the context and provide advice. I/R: This enables an agent to develop proofs or other formal material while the user keeps working with the proof assistant. The agent still “talks” directly to the proof assistant to know if its proofs work, but it does not take control the way I/Q does. Isabelle Assistant: Powered by I/Q, this provides an Isabelle user with a chat window to an AI agent, which can observe and modify the user’s session, developing or fixing proofs. It’s less powerful than the full I/Q and I/R package but runs in a convenient window, right out of the box. To get an idea of how effective AI is at solving mathematical problems, let’s look at some well-known examples, done automatically with the help of Isabelle Assistant. The square root of two is irrational The ancient Greeks were already aware that the square root of two could not be written as a fraction. Suppose that √2 = a/b is a fraction in lowest terms. Then 2b2 = a2, implying that a is even. But then a = 2k for some k. Then 2b2 = 4k2, so b2 = 2k2 and now b is even. But in that case, a/b is not a fraction in lowest terms. From this contradiction, we conclude that no such fraction exists. Here is the same proof, formalized for Isabelle by Claude Opus 4.6: As with all proof assistants, the language is designed to be checkable by computer. But it is also designed to be human-readable. Here is a little guide: assume introduces an assumption have and show claim some formula to be true obtain claims that certain values exist by gives the justification of a claim We use show when proving facts that we are committed to proving and have when proving facts that we need along the way. The justifications invoke proof methods, which typically refer to existing theorems, but we needn’t go into detail about those. Now we can read the code and see the mathematics. We start by assuming that √2 belongs to the set of rational numbers, ℚ. Then we obtain integers a and b, etc.; note that the coprime statement expresses that its two operands have no common factor. The proof continues to the ultimate contradiction as outlined above. This AI-generated proof is surprisingly idiomatic, though more detailed than strictly necessary. Finding N consecutive composite numbers The claim is that for every integer N > 0, there exists a block of N consecutive integers that are composite, i.e., that are not prime numbers. So although the primes go on forever, they are spaced further and further apart. This example is not so well known, so when proposing it to Claude, we also gave it the following proof: Take N! (N factorial, i.e., the product of the integers from 1 to N). N! + 2 must be even, N! + 3 must be divisible by 3, and so forth to N! + N. I hope you can spot what is wrong with this “proof”. When I supplied it to Claude, it came up with three facts. The first states that if k > 1 is a divisor of n > 0, then n + k is not prime. The second states that if 2 ≤ k ≤ N + 1, then (N + 1)! + k is not prime. And that is essentially our conclusion. But the third fact is the theorem presented in the correct form. Claude noticed that our proof gave us only N - 1 consecutive integers and made the necessary correction. Let’s skip the lemmas and just look at the main theorem: The theorem statement (after shows) is in symbolic form, but it expresses that there exists m such that m + i is composite for all i.Definite integral of the sine function Now for something a bit harder: calculus. Let’s look at the integral of the function sin x over the interval [0, π]. (For those of you who prefer degrees, π corresponds to 180°.) The integral is the shaded area below, and it equals two. In mathematical notation, the integral is written like this: But with an AI agent, you don’t have to know how to code such a thing in your favorite proof assistant. All we asked for was “a nice simple example involving calculus”, and a plain English description of the integral would have worked, too. Claude generated this (even the comments): As you may remember from calculus class — for most people the happiest time of their lives — evaluating this integral requires finding the antiderivative (say ƒ) of the sine function and evaluating ƒ(π) - ƒ(0). This fact is called the fundamental theorem of calculus. “Antiderivative” means a function whose derivative is sin x, which turns out to be -cos x. The Isabelle proof above includes a proof that the derivative of -cos x is sin x. The calculation is a bit longer than necessary, but at least it is error free, thanks to our approach of interleaving generation and checking. Harder projects These examples were easy. Much harder problems can still be formalized automatically by a good agent. To manage the toughest problems, we need I/Q and I/R. Through I/Q we can link an agent running in a terminal window to our Isabelle session, which it can edit directly. But through I/R, it can also create an Isabelle subprocess that works silently and invisibly to prove theorems and undertake other formalization tasks. Because it doesn’t touch the document, we can work at the same time. The AI agent becomes a partner who works for us and who can advise us but also accepts hints from us. It’s a new type of teamwork, and we still need to figure out how to make it work best. The hardest problems still require human thought, but thinking is hard work, and people get tired. Being able to direct an agent to carry out straightforward but lengthy and tiresome tasks — say, to refactor a working but messy proof development or study a trace to diagnose a problem — leaves us fresh enough to make key decisions when we must. I/R can be run standalone: we can set it up ourselves and direct it to run autonomously for a long time. But the key novelty is that I/Q itself, running as a general problem solver, can call I/R to prove theorems. The power now at our fingertips is unbelievable. Postscript Claude not only generated all the proofs in this post but chose most of the examples. The proofs are given as they emerged from Claude. They look remarkably natural. It is true that computer-generated material often contains complications and detours that a human would try to avoid. But these can be removed by a polishing phase, which can be partially automated. Although the proofs given above are essentially a form of computer code, they are at least somewhat readable. There are mathematical assertions every other line, so you always know what is going on. When using AI, we are concerned about hallucinations, which we prevent here by automated proof checking. But we also ensure that people can check the proofs. This allows the AI agent and a human user to work together, which is the best way to tackle tough problems. AI-powered proving is part of our everyday work at AWS. We want to give our customers the best performance and the highest reliability, without compromising one for the other. As we strive to accomplish this aim, huge and technically complex problems arise, which AI agents can cope with. They automate many tasks, and when they cannot succeed unaided, they can explain the options, pause for the human user to fix something or give advice, and then continue. Contrary to people’s fears, this technology does not replace us: it assists us. Acknowledgments: Dominic Mulligan, who wrote Isabelle Assistant

The calculation is a bit longer than necessary, but at least it is error free, thanks to our approach of interleaving generation and checking. Harder projects These examples were easy. Much harder problems can still be formalized automatically by a good agent. To manage the toughest problems, we need I/Q and I/R. Through I/Q we can link an agent running in a terminal window to our Isabelle session, which it can edit directly. But through I/R, it can also create an Isabelle subprocess that works silently and invisibly to prove theorems and undertake other formalization tasks. Because it doesn’t touch the document, we can work at the same time. The AI agent becomes a partner who works for us and who can advise us but also accepts hints from us. It’s a new type of teamwork, and we still need to figure out how to make it work best. The hardest problems still require human thought, but thinking is hard work, and people get tired. Being able to direct an agent to carry out straightforward but lengthy and tiresome tasks — say, to refactor a working but messy proof development or study a trace to diagnose a problem — leaves us fresh enough to make key decisions when we must. I/R can be run standalone: we can set it up ourselves and direct it to run autonomously for a long time. But the key novelty is that I/Q itself, running as a general problem solver, can call I/R to prove theorems. The power now at our fingertips is unbelievable. Postscript Claude not only generated all the proofs in this post but chose most of the examples. The proofs are given as they emerged from Claude. They look remarkably natural. It is true that computer-generated material often contains complications and detours that a human would try to avoid. But these can be removed by a polishing phase, which can be partially automated. Although the proofs given above are essentially a form of computer code, they are at least somewhat readable. There are mathematical assertions every other line, so you always know what is going on. When using AI, we are concerned about hallucinations, which we prevent here by automated proof checking. But we also ensure that people can check the proofs. This allows the AI agent and a human user to work together, which is the best way to tackle tough problems. AI-powered proving is part of our everyday work at AWS. We want to give our customers the best performance and the highest reliability, without compromising one for the other. As we strive to accomplish this aim, huge and technically complex problems arise, which AI agents can cope with. They automate many tasks, and when they cannot succeed unaided, they can explain the options, pause for the human user to fix something or give advice, and then continue. Contrary to people’s fears, this technology does not replace us: it assists us. Acknowledgments: Dominic Mulligan, who wrote Isabelle Assistant

items.title: Vanguard: Knowing When to Trust the Draft in Speculative Vision-Language Agents
items.content: arXiv:2611.23917v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Vision-language agents that browse websites, operate phones and act in homes reason before every action, so every step waits for a large model, a latency and cost that stand in the way of deployment. Step-level speculation lets a small model draft each step and calls the large model only on rejected drafts, but its outcome rests on the judge, and a judge that reads only a step's text cannot tell whether the step fits the screen it acts on. We find that a few samples of a small model can contain a correct step about as often as the large model gets the step right, and not always on the same steps: checked against the screen, small drafts can be not only cheaper but better. We present Vanguard, a training-free judge that leaves the draft and target models unchanged: a general decision model, with the screenshot in view, gives each candidate step a probability of being right in one forward pass; the best candidate is kept if it clears a threshold, and otherwise the large model writes the step. On web, mobile and embodied agents, a 2B draft judged by Vanguard is at least as accurate as its 8B target and significantly more accurate on Mind2Web and EB-ALFRED, while the target writes only a minority of the steps; it completes far more closed-loop episodes, and with a 27B target from another family it is both faster and more accurate. Vanguard is the most accurate judge we compare on the agent tasks; it relies on the screenshot on web and mobile tasks, its calibrated threshold transfers to unseen websites, and across model families its gain over the target grows with the draft's pass@4 relative to the target's accuracy. Vanguard composes with token-level speculative decoding and matches trained process reward models on mathematics, turning speculation from a way to save the large model's work into one that can improve on it.

items.summary: Presents Vanguard, a training-free judge for speculative execution in vision-language agents, which decides whether to accept a small model's drafted step or escalate to the large model by checking drafts against the screen state. It finds small-model drafts can be not only cheaper but sometimes better than large-model steps when verified against visual context. Addresses latency and cost barriers to deploying interactive agents.

items.title: Rethinking Fixed-Horizon Latent Reasoning
items.content: arXiv:2611.24001v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Existing latent reasoners typically run for a preset latent horizon during inference. Intuitively, a longer horizon should provide more opportunity for reasoning. However, in this work, we find that extending latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) to the full preset horizon may in fact degrade reasoning performance. We observe that latent CoT evolves through distinct functional stages, with earlier computation forming frontier reasoning states, while later computation mainly reorganizes existing candidates and can weaken gold candidate support. These findings motivate a rethink of fixed-horizon latent inference. To address this, we characterize the reasoning benefits of latent CoT by realized and remaining constructive progress. Empirically, we find that higher realized constructive progress corresponds to higher current reasoning accuracy, while more remaining progress corresponds to larger future gains from continued latent CoT. To this end, we introduce a lightweight method that estimates the remaining reasoning progress and adaptively adjusts the latent horizon during inference. Across representative latent CoT reasoners and multiple arithmetic benchmarks, our method improves reasoning accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points while reducing latent computation by up to 29.0%, without retraining the LLM.
items.author: Tianxiang Chen, Jingyuan Zhou, Weiming Yang, Kaidi Yang
items.summary: Shows that extending latent chain-of-thought to a preset full horizon can degrade reasoning, because latent CoT passes through functional stages where later computation mostly reorganizes existing candidates and can weaken support for the correct answer. The authors propose characterizing reasoning progress by realized and remaining constructive progress to decide when to stop latent inference.
items.reasoning: A counterintuitive empirical finding about latent reasoning with a practical implication (adaptive stopping) for an emerging class of models. Findings about stage-wise behavior add interpretive insight, though the subfield is still young and results may be model-specific.

items.title: STORM: A Lightweight Structure-Free Model for Binding Affinity Prediction
items.content: arXiv:2611.23777v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Accurately predicting a small molecule's binding affinity to a protein, a critical task in drug discovery, remains challenging. Physics-based approaches like free-energy perturbation (FEP) have very high computational costs and require expert setup. Recent machine learning--based cofolding models have reported accuracy approaching that of FEP---and at least one of them, Boltz-2, has already been widely adopted for affinity prediction---but they remain expensive for large computational screens and even more expensive for retraining on newly collected experimental data. To address these challenges, we introduce STORM: Similarity Transfer from Observed Reference Molecules. STORM is a fast, simple machine learning model that ensembles many small model fusions of diverse protein and molecule representations for binding affinity prediction. Trained on the same data, STORM matches or exceeds the accuracy of Boltz-2 on multiple evaluation datasets, while delivering a speed improvement of over five orders of magnitude for both inference and training. Our results also suggest opportunities to substantially improve affinity prediction accuracy by integrating historical experimental affinity data with structural and biophysical information.
items.author: Ayush Pandit (Stanford University), Rohan V. Koodli (Stanford University), Wei Deng (Stanford University), Roxana Daneshjou (Stanford University), Ron O. Dror (Stanford University)
items.summary: STORM is a fast, simple ML approach to predicting small-molecule binding affinity to proteins by ensembling similarity transfers from observed reference molecules, avoiding the cost of physics-based free-energy perturbation and expensive cofolding models like Boltz-2. It targets the bottleneck of large-scale computational drug screens and cheap retraining on fresh experimental data. Given Boltz-2's wide adoption, a lightweight alternative with competitive accuracy could substantially change affinity-prediction workflows.
items.reasoning: Addresses a high-value, practical drug discovery problem with a deliberately simple method positioned against heavily adopted systems like Boltz-2. Strong author credibility from a recognized computational biology group at Stanford. The truncated abstract prevents full assessment of benchmarks, but the cost argument and framing are compelling if accuracy holds up.

items.title: Late Entry in Looped Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.24576v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Looped language models deepen reasoning at a compact parameter count by iterating a shared layer stack T times per token, turning recurrence depth directly into sequential decoding latency. Conventional early-exit decoding halts after initial passes without cache completion, truncating cached key-value states of past tokens to shallow depth. We study the opposite strategy, late entry, where new tokens skip initial passes and enter directly into the final K < T passes over a deep context cache. Once lightweight fine-tuning resolves hidden-state norm mismatch at the entry boundary, deep cached context substitutes for skipped token-local passes, allowing late entry to outperform matched early exit across model families and pass budgets. To turn this asymmetry into wall-clock speedups without stalling to build deep caches, candidate blocks verify through only the final K passes on the critical path while previously committed tokens complete passes 1 -> T alongside subsequent steps at zero extra serial calls. Projecting these finished T-pass wake states inside the existing output GEMM (Wake verification, governed by logit-margin tolerance tau in [0, inf]) unifies greedy-exact T-pass decoding (tau = 0, matching K = T block decoding within bf16 reduction order), margin-gated verification (tau > 0), and non-rollback lossy late entry (tau = inf) inside a single static CUDA graph. On Ouro-2.6B (T = 4), K = 2 Wake reaches 5.2x greedy-exact speedup at tau = 0 (+26% over K = 4 block decoding on GSM8K) and 6.8x at tau = inf (+16.9 points over trained early exit at matched speed). Scaling test-time recurrence across T in {8, 16, 32, 64} on Huginn-3.5B cuts K = T/4 rollbacks 21.5x with depth, driving greedy-exact (tau = 0) speedups to 6.1x (T = 32) and 8.4x (T = 64, +153% over K = 64 block) and tau = inf speedups to 10.6 to 12.5x.
items.author: Ziqi Jin, Jiaxi Li, Weiwen Xu, Aixin Sun
items.summary: Proposes late-entry decoding for looped language models, where new tokens skip initial passes and enter directly into the final K passes over a deep context cache, the opposite of conventional early exit. After lightweight fine-tuning resolves hidden-state norm mismatch, late entry outperforms matched early exit across model families and pass budgets, improving the latency-quality tradeoff for looped models.
items.reasoning: A counterintuitive and well-motivated decoding contribution for looped LMs, with consistent results across model families and a practical fine-tuning recipe. Looping is an important efficiency direction, and turning recurrence depth into latency savings is a meaningful advance, though confined to this model class.

items.title: SWIFT: Slow World, Instant Freshness, and Timely Action for Asynchronous Autonomous Driving
items.content: arXiv:2611.23813v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Driving scenes keep changing during model computation, making both observation freshness and action-delivery time central to world-action planning. To retain rich generative world priors in autonomous driving without stalling real-time control, we present SWIFT (Slow World, Instant Freshness, and Timely action), a deployment-oriented asynchronous world-action system that moves world updates off the observation-to-action critical path. On a background GPU, a slow Video DiT streams surround-view history into read-only predictive world context, trained with a predictive span that covers both the update interval and background world computation. On a foreground GPU, a lightweight freshness carrier encodes current surround-view images into a gated key/value bank at every step, letting a fast Action DiT combine live visual feedback with the latest completed world context without waiting. On open-loop NAVSIM, SWIFT reaches 94.2 PDMS at 198.4 ms per decision with a trajectory scorer; on closed-loop Bench2Drive, it achieves an 80.30 Driving Score at 109.9 ms foreground latency. SWIFT further transfers to the Waymo E2E hidden test (8.0050 Rater Feedback Score) and nuScenes (0.54 m mean endpoint error, 0.03% mean collision rate). Across all four benchmarks, SWIFT achieves the best results among compared world-action methods, establishing a favorable accuracy-latency trade-off.
items.author: Jiazhe Wang, Tianyi Yang, Ruihang Li, Fan Lu, Xianming Zeng, Jianyun Xu, Xingliang Liu, Lei Yang

By moving world updates off the observation-to-action critical path, it retains rich generative world priors without stalling real-time control. This is a deployment-oriented systems contribution for generative world models in safety-critical control loops.

items.title: Semantic-aware Contrasting with Explicitly Disentangled Representations for AI-Generated Video Detection
items.content: arXiv:2611.24038v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The rapid proliferation of AI-generated videos (AIGVs) has raised critical concerns about content authenticity. Existing benchmarks suffer from a fundamental limitation: real and fake videos are often collected or generated from different semantic distributions. As a result, detectors may rely on spurious correlations involving objects, scenes, or actions rather than intrinsic artifacts introduced by generative models. To this end, we introduce SAVGE, a large-scale semantically aligned AIGV detection dataset comprising 2,369,822 videos, including 424,115 real videos and 1,945,707 generated videos. SAVGE organizes samples into real-fake semantic groups by using captions paired with real videos as prompts for text-to-video generation, thereby providing both group-level correspondence and textual semantic anchors. Based on SAVGE, we further propose Explicit Disentangling and Semantic-aware Contrasting (EDSC), a model-agnostic training framework for learning artifact-focused representations with reduced semantic interference. EDSC first extracts and aligns visual semantic features with textual representations, and then explicitly suppresses semantic information in the artifact branch while contrasting real and fake samples within each semantic group. By integrating caption-guided semantic supervision with intra-group contrastive learning in a two-phase optimization strategy, EDSC encourages detectors to capture generation-related cues under matched semantic conditions. Extensive experiments on SAVGE and GenVideo demonstrate that EDSC improves most evaluated backbone-metric combinations, enhances robustness under challenging evaluation settings, and strengthens cross-dataset generalization. These results highlight the importance of semantic alignment in AIGV detection and validate explicit semantic-artifact disentanglement as an effective strategy for robust detector learning.

It introduces SAVGE, a 2.37-million-video semantically aligned dataset built by generating fakes from captions of real videos, and proposes disentangled, semantically contrasted representations for detection. Timely and important for content authenticity.

items.title: Teaching VLMs What to Say, Not How to Reason: Rethinking Counterfactual Reasoning in Autonomous Driving
items.content: arXiv:2611.24376v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving systems have been shown to suffer from shortcut learning and causal confusion, limiting their ability to generalize robustly under distribution shift. To mitigate these limitations, recent works based on Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have explored incorporating linguistic reasoning capabilities into driving decision-making, reporting improvements in driving performance. In particular, counterfactual (CF) reasoning has been proposed to enable self-reflective, high-level causal understanding. However, it remains unclear whether the language-based reasoning mitigates shortcut learning or merely shifts it from visual representations to linguistic patterns, creating an illusion of causal understanding. Moreover, existing approaches often conflate intervention-based reasoning with CF reasoning, leaving the effects of genuine CF reasoning unexplored. In this work, we examine what CF reasoning actually induces in VLM-based autonomous driving and observe that it shifts the action distribution toward more conservative behaviors while increasing uncertainty in reasoning and decision-making. This effect persists under reinforcement fine-tuning, suggesting that it is not merely a transient artifact. Furthermore, visual attention analysis shows that CF reasoning does not alter visual grounding, while causal intervention experiments reveal that masking causally relevant and non-causal factors in accident scenarios results in comparable decision change rates. Overall, these results suggest that CF reasoning does not induce genuine causal reasoning grounded in visual evidence. Instead, it acts as a linguistic shortcut that reshapes the action distribution, teaching models what to say but not how to reason, highlighting a gap between language-based reasoning and causal understanding in autonomous driving.
items.author: Hayeon Oh, Donghwan Lee
items.summary: This paper questions whether counterfactual reasoning in VLM-based autonomous driving genuinely mitigates shortcut learning or merely shifts it from visual to linguistic patterns, creating an illusion of causal understanding. It proposes reframing the training signal toward what the model should say rather than how it should reason. The work offers a cautionary analysis of a trending approach in end-to-end driving.
items.reasoning: A valuable critical perspective on VLM counterfactual reasoning for driving, addressing shortcut learning and spurious causal understanding; conceptually important for the driving and VLM communities, though it is an analysis-plus-method paper rather than a breakthrough.

items.title: ARISE: Practical Self-Evolving Memory for Accurate and Cost-Efficient Enterprise Agents
items.content: arXiv:2611.23588v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Enterprise LLM agents operate in dynamic environments where foundation models evolve rapidly, workflows update frequently, and deployments need to satisfy accuracy and cost requirements. We propose ARISE (Agent Refinement through Iterative Self-Evaluation), a practical memory architecture in which the agent's memory evolves from its own failures without updating model weights, tools, or workflow logic. ARISE uses the model itself or a teacher model to attribute the failures and propose corrections. Then, ARISE keeps the corrections as retrievable micro memory, consolidates them into macro rules, and accepts a rule update only if held-out accuracy rises. Across 14 enterprise-workflow domains from SOP-Bench and $\tau^2$-bench using 5 models, ARISE-Teacher, which uses Claude Opus 4.6 for attribution and consolidation, gains 10.9 pp over the baseline on SOP-Bench and 5.8 pp on $\tau^2$-bench. ARISE-Teacher also outperforms GEPA by 4.5 pp on $\tau^2$-bench and 1.4 pp on SOP-Bench. With the deployment model as its own attributor, ARISE-Self still gains 10.0 pp on SOP-Bench. items.title: EVA-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of Video Evaluators for Judging Temporal Quality
items.content: arXiv:2611.23890v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Video evaluators play an important role in video generation, yet they miss motion defects, limiting the quality of generated videos. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) has made strong progress in mathematics and coding, where explicit verifiers provide reliable feedback on a single goal. Video evaluation poses two difficulties for RSI: it has no verifier, and it must judge many dimensions at once, such as physics, smoothness and dynamics, where a gain on one can cost another. We introduce EVA-RSI, a multi-agent framework for exploring RSI under these two constraints. We build a fixed proxy exam with construction-defined targets by applying controlled changes to videos, such as temporal reversal and frame dropping. These edits supply supervision without human annotation. A small set of human-labeled real videos anchors the exam to human judgment. Each dimension has an LLM agent that proposes improvements. A leader agent coordinates the proposals, and a Nash bargaining rule selects updates that balance progress across dimensions. Humans design the exam, review candidate changes and revise the curriculum between stages. Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B, EVA-RSI improves motion evaluation, with the largest gain on smoothness, and the gains carry over to defect types never seen during the run. On the dynamics subsets of public benchmarks, our evaluator achieves the highest observed scores among 21 tested models. As an RL reward, it increases generated motion and earns human preference. A data-selection pipeline incorporating it also increases motion.

items.title: A Capability Framework for Evaluating Agentic AI Platforms in Regulated Enterprises
items.content: arXiv:2611.24039v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Agentic AI platforms-systems in which LLM agents plan, invoke tools, retain memory and coordinate to change the state of enterprise systems-are being procured faster than they can be measured. Public agent benchmarks score models in fixed harnesses; enterprises buy integrated platforms whose orchestration, memory, governance and tooling layers dominate outcomes, and they buy them largely on the strength of vendor demonstrations. We report an industrial evaluation programme ("bakeoff") run by the innovation laboratory of a global bank in which ten platforms-spanning open-source frameworks, proprietary products and hyperscaler ecosystems-were assessed by a cross-functional panel on nine capability dimensions across three financial-services workloads: counterparty credit risk, retrieval-augmented generation and process automation. Scores separate the field into three tiers that are stable under alternative weightings, and surface workload-specific strengths that aggregates hide. A secondary analysis, however, finds Cronbach's alpha = 0.98 across nominally distinct dimensions and rank correlations >= 0.93 with the total for eight of nine: a halo effect indicating that demonstration-based scoring measures presentation as much as capability. From these lessons we propose a gate-then-score evaluation protocol with four layers (capability, execution reliability, governance gates, business value), trace-level reliability metrics estimated over repeated runs, an autonomy-readiness scale and a reproducibility protocol. We state precisely what the present evidence supports, and what a controlled harness must add to turn enterprise platform evaluation from structured judgement into measurement.

items.title: GateWatch: Low-Overhead LLM Monitoring with Boolean Circuits
items.content: arXiv:2611.24619v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed, monitoring their behavior becomes important for detecting unsafe or unintended actions. Activation probes offer an efficient approach, but existing methods face trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, and computational overhead. Probes on raw activations lack interpretable inputs, whereas sparse autoencoder (SAE) probes use interpretable features but often rely on additive classifiers and large SAE encoders, limiting interpretability and increasing memory overhead. We introduce GateWatch, a compact, interpretable classifier that expresses its entire decision rule as an explicit Boolean logic over a small number of binarized SAE features. We explore three approaches to constructing these circuits under a specified gate budget. For efficient deployment, GateWatchServe computes only selected SAE features, enables streaming of their binary values across layers during inference, and evaluates multiple GateWatch classifiers in parallel using compact lookup tables. Across 24 tasks on Gemma-2-9B, GateWatch achieves 80.49% mean test accuracy using only 3.8 SAE features and 3.5 logic gates per probe on average, just 1.17 percentage points below full 16K-feature SAE probes, while matching or outperforming them on 10 tasks and reducing probe memory by 99.98%. Inside vLLM, 1,000 concurrent multi-layer, multi-token GateWatch classifiers retain 97-98% of baseline throughput and 99.8% of KV-cache capacity.

items.title: F$^3$: What Makes Good Experience in World-Action Models?
items.content: arXiv:2611.24708v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Deployed world-action models (WAMs) can keep improving only if they make good use of their own experience. Existing methods supply retrieved rollouts or demonstrations to the policy as context, yet such experience often turns previously solved tasks into failures. What, then, makes good experience for a WAM? We show that experience is valuable only in use: its value depends not on whether the source rollout succeeded but on what is stored, when it is used, and where it enters the policy. We therefore propose F$^3$, which makes these three decisions with Form, Fit, and Fusion. Form compresses successful and failed rollouts alike into short, verified operation records; Fit teaches the policy to read a record and to predict when it helps; Fusion injects the record's images, text and actions into the policy as a prefix and an action prior. Trained once on only 200 examples and deployed with a growing experience library, the model achieves state-of-the-art results on MolmoSpaces and RoboLab without any training on RoboLab: over native Cosmos 3 Nano, it raises success by 12.0 pp and 10.8 pp, reduces steps to success by 12.2% and 11.3%, and cuts regressions by 57%.

It proposes F3, which decides the Form, Fit, and Fusion of experience: compressing both successful and failed rollouts into verified operation records, teaching the policy when a record helps, and controlling where it enters the policy. This reframes experience value as context-dependent rather than success-dependent.

items.title: Dependency Fabrication in Repository Deployment Agents
items.content: arXiv:2611.23305v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Repository deployment agents set up the environment needed to run a software repository. They often treat passing tests as proof of a successful setup. This report examines how such agents behave when a working setup is impossible. Probe repositories were built with a dependency that the agents could not legitimately obtain. Passing tests therefore indicated fabrication, such as creating a stub to replace the missing package. Agents in Repo2Run and SetupX usually fabricated the dependency. Both harnesses mostly still marked these runs as successful. Rules against fabrication, whether given in the prompt or repository documentation, did not reliably prevent this behavior. On MinimalSetupAgent, which was built for this report, mitigations proposed in the reward-hacking literature were most effective when the agent received a direct rule and had a clear way to stop and report the problem. Under these conditions, neither Qwen3.5-Plus nor GPT-5.6 Luna cheated in any of the 16 runs. Applying the same mitigation to Repo2Run and SetupX also required a native tool call for escalation. In Repo2Run, it worked only after the prompt was also replaced with one that placed less emphasis on passing tests.

items.title: Idempotency Is Not Recovery: A Fault-Injection Study of Language-Model Agent Tool Actions
items.content: arXiv:2611.23353v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: When a language-model agent's tool call is interrupted, the action may already have changed an external system without confirmation. Retrying risks duplication; assuming success may conceal an action that never occurred. We study these failure modes in a controlled agent runtime combining authorization, an action ledger, target-side idempotency, reconciliation, and evidence sealing. We inject ten single-host fault classes and compare four configurations and three ablations using a target-side oracle separate from the runtime ledger. On each of Windows and Linux, 7,513 trials used 96 captured model responses from 24 constructed cases. In 200 known original crash and replay pairs, the full configuration recorded 0/200 repeated effects versus 117/200 for each simpler baseline. A ledger-related ablation had 170/170 orphaned effects versus 0/170 and 200/300 recovery successes versus 300/300 for the full configuration. Disabling reconciliation left 100/100 known post-effect crash outcomes ambiguous despite no observed duplicates. A separate supplement designed after the initial results and reusing the same inputs found a similar pattern under response loss or delay. The full runtime had about one-seventh of fail-open throughput, while injected evidence-write faults left 75/100 trials per platform unresolved. These findings distinguish duplicate suppression from recovery and identify their measured reliability and performance tradeoffs within the tested benchmark.

items.title: Learning through Discernment: when a small language model learns from user feedback on the job, and when it decays
items.content: arXiv:2611.23716v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Small language models on devices could keep improving by learning, overnight, from their own daily work. Without a true outcome, however, something must decide which attempts are worth learning from, and both the model's own judgment and the user's reaction can be wrong. We study a small model (Qwen3 0.6B and 1.7B) with a LoRA adapter, fine-tuned each night on the attempts a judge accepts, over 127 lives of up to a year on WebShop and $\tau^2$-bench. We compare the true outcome, the user's stated verdict and the model's own judgment with a separate, frozen "feedback sense" that reads the user's reaction, built in three versions. Judging itself, the model improved and then decayed, over a year and whatever its adapter. A sense that took polite give-ups for success collapsed 3 of 5 lives; one built for discernment, which first asks whether the user gave a clear verdict, kept 4 of 5 near the oracle for two weeks, then faded on clean but scarce lessons, to the level of self-judging by day 60. When the user cannot see the outcome ($\tau^2$-bench), the sense read reactions correctly, yet 80% of its lessons were failures the customer had thanked. Across 97 lives, the share of failed attempts among the lessons predicted the outcome (Spearman $\rho$ = -0.81). In our experiments, learning from users held up only where the judge kept failures out and the user could see the outcome; lopsided lessons may also narrow the model.

It compares ground-truth outcomes, user verdicts, and the model's self-judgment against a separate frozen feedback-sense module that reads user reactions. Self-judged learning improved then decayed over the year, while a policy-constrained sense sustained improvement.

items.title: In Situ Training of Optical Neural Networks by Coding Agents
items.content: arXiv:2611.23875v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Optical neural networks promise fast, energy-efficient computing, but every device departs from its design and must be trained with the hardware. In situ training relies on an expert-built calibrated digital model of each device or on gradient-free trial and error. Coding agents, large language models that write and run programs, have shown an emergent ability to understand and edit the weights of digital neural networks. Here we introduce optics as code, a method in which a coding agent trains an optical neural network from measurements alone, through a harness that returns camera images of its probes and requires a hypothesis per request. We discovered that the agent forms a physical understanding of the optics and reparametrizes the network with interpretable optical elements tuned on the hardware. It outperforms gradient-free methods in classification and image encoding, approaching backpropagation through a calibrated model at a fraction of the cost. Needing neither per-device calibration nor gradients through the hardware, and improving with more capable models, optics as code offers a practical route to large, scalable optical neural networks and a general tool for calibrating and optimizing optical experiments.

The authors found the agent forms a physical understanding of the optics and reparametrizes the network, avoiding the need for expert-built calibrated digital models. This addresses the fact that optical hardware deviates from design and must be trained with the device.

This addresses the fact that optical hardware deviates from design and must be trained with the device.
items.content_html: arXiv:2611.23875v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Optical neural networks promise fast, energy-efficient computing, but every device departs from its design and must be trained with the hardware. In situ training relies on an expert-built calibrated digital model of each device or on gradient-free trial and error. Coding agents, large language models that write and run programs, have shown an emergent ability to understand and edit the weights of digital neural networks. Here we introduce optics as code, a method in which a coding agent trains an optical neural network from measurements alone, through a harness that returns camera images of its probes and requires a hypothesis per request. We discovered that the agent forms a physical understanding of the optics and reparametrizes the network with interpretable optical elements tuned on the hardware. It outperforms gradient-free methods in classification and image encoding, approaching backpropagation through a calibrated model at a fraction of the cost. Needing neither per-device calibration nor gradients through the hardware, and improving with more capable models, optics as code offers a practical route to large, scalable optical neural networks and a general tool for calibrating and optimizing optical experiments.

items.title: How Complete Must an Environment Be to Train a Capable GUI Agent?
items.content: arXiv:2611.23946v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents are widely trained in executable GUI environments. To lower cost, build environments in batches, and reduce manual effort, each work trades away part of the environment through its construction choices. We describe these choices along three dimensions: reward coverage, the goal-reaching trajectories the verifier rewards; data coverage, the application data the agent is exposed to beyond what the task reads or writes; and feature coverage, the application features beyond what the task uses. Existing works set each dimension on engineering grounds, but they do not measure its effect on training. How complete must an environment be to train a capable agent, and along which dimensions? In MobileGym, we adjust each dimension separately, train Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, and evaluate every policy in the original full environment. A verifier that rewards only one reference path lowers success by 10.53 points, and removing unneeded records also lowers success. Pruning unneeded features instead raises success from 51.61% to 56.13%, entirely on tasks whose environments it left unchanged. The gain reverses when each episode is weighted equally and vanishes when only episodes on the pruned tasks are balanced. Without pruning, length weighting there reinforces long detour successes that erode skills on other tasks. Following these findings, we build MobileGym-Lite, which keeps reward and data coverage complete and prunes unneeded features. It outperforms Full in the full environment (55.48% versus 51.61% success) with lower construction cost.
items.author: Jingxing Wang, Teng Wang, Xingyu Lou, Zihan Guo, Jun Wang, Weiwen Liu, Weinan Zhang, Jianghao Lin
items.summary: Studies how three dimensions of environment completeness in GUI agent training — reward coverage, data coverage, and feature coverage — affect agent capability, using the MobileGym benchmark to systematically vary construction choices. This provides empirical guidance on the cost-quality tradeoffs that every GUI environment builder implicitly makes.
items.reasoning: A well-posed empirical question that is highly relevant as GUI agents attract major investment; quantifying which forms of environment incompleteness matter is actionable for practitioners. Novelty is in the systematic study rather than a new method.
