items.title: Conceptual full-vehicle modeling of a modular all-wheel-drive robotic ADS test platform as a foundation for a digital twin architecture
items.content: arXiv:2611.24646v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper presents the development of an initial full-vehicle simulation model of the PixKit modular electric test platform in IPG CarMaker. The objective is to create a physics-based and extendable model structure that can serve as a low-level foundation for future digital twin applications. The reference vehicle is a skateboard chassis combining unconventional vehicle characteristics such as four independent wheel-hub motors and rear axle steering capable of high steering angles. Since complete measurement data of the vehicle is not yet available, the model parameterization is based on a combination of manufacturer documentation, derived values and engineering assumptions. The modeling approach focuses on the system-level integration of the main vehicle subsystems rather than on a fully validated representation. The resulting model was assessed through basic driving scenarios with different steering inputs and configurations. The simulations showed stable model behavior and physically plausible interaction between the subsystems. The all-wheel-drive configuration produced symmetric wheel responses in longitudinal driving, while counter-phase rear axle steering increased the yaw response and reduced the simulated turning circle diameter compared with front axle steering only. The circular driving scenario further indicated bounded roll and slip behavior. Overall, the implemented CarMaker model provides a traceable and functional simulation basis for the PixKit vehicle. It can support future model refinement, calibration with real vehicle data and development with the goal of creating a validated digital twin architecture.

items.title: I'm worried about LLMs accelerating hardware for cheap ASI
items.content:
Basically:

- You could probably make a superintelligent AI with some currently unknown new paradigm for <$10k if you had the right hardware and algorithms
- Plausibly this would be much easier and faster with better hardware
- LLMs will make developers of novel-paradigm AI systems really good at hardware creation and design
- This seems bad, because those novel-paradigm AIs seem unlikely to be aligned with human values

## ASI could in principle be created cheaply

I think it's very plausible that with the right hardware and algorithms someone could make a wildly superintelligent AI model extremely cheaply (<$10k in energy cost), for roughly the reasons described in this post (although I think it underestimates how useful hardware improvements will be for building ASI). Basically, I think that given that you can train a human from nothing to a 20-year-old for less than $10k worth of electricity, you should expect to be able to train an AI to a similar level for the same amount of electricity with the right hardware and algorithms. In fact you should be able to do that much more efficiently, since you only care about intelligence and don't need to worry about powering a whole human body. And if you're making your own brain it's probably pretty doable to just make it bigger.

I don't think we'll get to this kind of novel ASI through iteratively improving current AI paradigms, but instead using something that's very different than current LLMs. To be clear, I also think that scaling LLMs could get us to superintelligence. I'm worried that ASI will be created through some novel paradigm first though.

### Probably misaligned

items.title: KnowMe Paper Radar: Lightweight Discovery of Promising Papers in the Age of Autoresearch
items.content: arXiv:2611.23702v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The growing volume of topically similar papers makes it difficult to identify new work that can offer useful research insights or methodological guidance. We present KnowMe Paper Radar, a lightweight discovery tool that combines multiple sources of evidence into personalized reading priorities. Users specify topics, priorities, exclusions and dates; the system brings together topical relevance, recency, author research histories, collaboration paths and direction-specific institutional context. By exposing each score component and its supporting sources, KnowMe helps readers select promising papers for their current questions and discover relevant work beyond familiar authors. Automatic acquisition, version merging and graph-cache reuse keep this workflow convenient without large language model (LLM) inference during ordinary use. Experiments on 174,640 acquired records show more than threefold faster repeated context preparation, while cached abstracts improve normalized discounted cumulative gain at rank 10 (NDCG@10) from 0.412 to 0.598 on expert-judged retrieval tasks. Complementary analyses examine how the same accumulated records support semantic retrieval, research-history modeling and literature-grounded planning. A browser interface and a structured command-line interface (CLI) make these capabilities available to both researchers and research agents, positioning KnowMe as a practical upstream tool for literature-informed recursive self-improvement (RSI) workflows.

It targets the problem of identifying useful papers amid rapidly growing, topically similar literature. Automatic acquisition, version merging, and graph caching keep it lightweight.

items.title: The Largest Tractable Subclass of Multi-Scale Allen Temporal Reasoning
items.content: arXiv:2611.24498v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel model for temporal reasoning over multi-scale intervals. We show that this model yields a complete reasoning framework and exhibits other particularly interesting properties. Furthermore, we identify the maximal tractable subalgebra for this model, as well as for the other complete model, in the qualitative scales context, which exhibits weaker properties but whose results can be derived by transfer from our new model.

items.title: LAaDT-DSS: decision support for non-experts on rooftop PV, incentive and grid simulations under Turkish tariff rules
items.content: arXiv:2611.24810v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Rooftop photovoltaics raise three questions: should a household invest, which incentive costs the state least, and does the feeder stay within limits? Those who ask are rarely modellers. We present LAaDT-DSS, decision-support software that answers all three under Turkish tariff rules from one simulation core. Non-experts reach it by clicking a house on a 3D map or by asking in plain words; a language model is asked to call the simulation tools, not to compute. Each entry of its 125-entry parameter registry is marked as sourced or estimated. Case studies test the system. Its PV yield lies within $\pm$3.6% of two independent tools at equal losses. Across 2,048 draws of its estimated inputs, the answer for PV alone held in all but one; with a battery, it changed in 31-41% of the draws. Four scripted chat scenarios ran end to end; no user study was run.

items.summary: LAaDT-DSS is decision-support software letting non-experts assess rooftop photovoltaic investment, state incentive costs, and feeder limits under Turkish tariffs via a 3D map or natural language, with an LLM calling simulation tools rather than computing directly. It includes a 125-entry sourced/estimated parameter registry and validation showing PV yield within 3.6% of two independent tools plus sensitivity analysis over 2,048 draws.
items.reasoning: Well-engineered domain-specific tool with sensible LLM-as-tool-caller design and honest uncertainty reporting, but narrow applicability to one national policy context and limited research novelty.

items.title: Basic Problems With the Chip Security Act
items.content:
Epistemic status: I have no experience in law or anything, I just read this bill and noticed some issues. This is not deeply researched.

[Crossposted from my blog, BlueprintingHeaven.]

Here is my attempt at preventing these problems from being overlooked. I am not a US citizen, so if you are, please do what I cannot.

Briefly, the Chip Security Act is about making sure chips aren't getting smuggled into places they're not supposed to be. A mix of ping-based location verification, inspections, and other things is proposed. It is currently being negotiated as part of the annual defence bill, the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), which basically always gets passed. The final text is expected to be released this December.

I am looking at the version passed by the House Foreign Affairs Committee in March 2026.

Issue number one is the inspections are listed as "periodic". Issue number two is the super long timeframes given for some requirements, some of them longer than my AI timelines.

Periodic inspections are mentioned here:

The term ‘‘chip security mechanism’’ means a software-, firmware-, or hardware-enabled security mechanism or a physical security mechanism, including—

(A) periodic on-site audits or inventories at the end-user’s approved destination for the covered integrated circuit product;

(Note that inspections are optional: they're one choice of ~4, and as long as one of them is done, that counts. Which one is done is decided by Commerce. Ping-based location verification is another example of an option.) The word periodic does not necessarily imply inspections with regular time intervals, but it's certainly not strict enough to imply random inspections. Inspections have to be random, or very short notice, otherwise the entities being inspected can move incriminating objects off-site before the auditors arrive. This is super basic and obvious and it's what you do for nuclear inspections![1]...

items.summary: A non-lawyer's close reading of the Chip Security Act (House Foreign Affairs Committee version, March 2026), identifying weaknesses such as only 'periodic' inspections and compliance timeframes longer than the author's AI timelines. The bill, under negotiation in the NDAA, concerns location verification and inspection mechanisms to prevent chip smuggling.

items.title: Surplus and profit: rethinking unfairness
items.content:
People around me sometimes complain that quant firms get paid a lot while contributing little (some even claim negative) to the world. I also sense the "unfairness", but it's pretty hard to actually explain how that feeling arises. In this post, I try to describe a hypothesis on where that feeling comes from, and argue that big tech and frontier labs have their own versions of it, which some people also complain is "unfair".

I don't have a finished theory. What I have is one idea and three places where I see it.

# Profit as a proxy

Capitalism works well partly because profit is a decent proxy for contribution. Profit originates from making something people value more than it costs (i.e. "surplus"), and you keep some of it as profit. Usually you keep only a small part, and the rest goes to customers or society. Nordhaus (2004) estimated that innovators in the US captured only about 2% of the total value their innovations created.

From this point of view, people might feel it is unfair if the above is not true. I see at least two main ways things could go wrong:

- The firm keeps an unusually large share of the surplus it creates.
- The firm causes harms or uses inputs it doesn't pay for.

## 1. Apple farmer as the base case

I like to use apple farmers as an illustration of what people would normally expect about a business's contribution and its profit. To the best of my knowledge, the grower gets roughly 25–30% of the retail price, and has to pay for land and labor, making it barely profitable and volatile. (The grocer isn't getting rich either: US supermarkets keep about 1–2% of sales as net profit.)...

The author applies this frame to the AI industry, invoking Nordhaus's estimate that innovators capture only about 2 percent of the value they create.

items.title: Beyond Corpus-Driven Imitation: Evolving Musical Mindsets in the Agentic Orchestra via Quantum Reinforcement Learning
items.content: arXiv:2611.24290v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper presents a framework for computer-aided music composition and performance based on quantum reinforcement learning and multi-agent interaction. We introduce the agentic orchestra, where musical agents evolve distinct mindsets through trial-and-error engagement with a musical environment, rather than through training on large datasets. The agents are implemented as parameterised quantum circuits. They evolve distinct compositional behaviours, referred to as mindsets. This enables the exploration of musical decision spaces using quantum superposition and entanglement within a hybrid quantum-classical loop. We present two complementary agent architectures: atomistic agents, which process pitch and rhythm independently, and holistic agents, which handle pitch and duration as unified note events. items.title: Management of Behavioral Addictions via Artificial Intelligence based Digital Technologies
items.content: arXiv:2611.23341v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Behavioral addictions, such as problematic gaming, gambling, social media use, and online shopping, have emerged as a growing global concern with significant psychological, social, and economic consequences. Traditional assessment and treatment approaches, while clinically grounded, often struggle with scalability, accessibility, and long-term engagement. In recent years, advances in digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) have enabled the development of novel, data-driven solutions for the prevention, detection, treatment, and recovery of behavioral addictions. This book presents a comprehensive survey of the management of behavioral addictions through digital technologies, bridging clinical foundations with state-of-the-art computational approaches. This book aims to provide researchers, clinicians, and practitioners with a unified, interdisciplinary perspective on the opportunities and limitations of AI-based digital technologies in behavioral addiction management,and to highlight pathways toward more scalable, personalized, and effective intervention strategies.

items.title: Sparse designs via quantization of the uniform measure on high-dimensional hypercubes
items.content: arXiv:2611.24507v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: While the notions of sphere packing and sphere covering underlie the most widely used criteria for space-filling design in computer experiments, namely, the maximin and minimax approaches, they suffer from major drawbacks in high dimensions. First, when the dimension $d$ is very large, deploying a space-filling design requires an extremely large number of design points, making the very notion of a space-filling design questionable. Second, these two design characteristics are highly sensitive to boundaries, particularly when the design domain is a hypercube (the case considered in this paper), and especially to its vertices. This sensitivity is particularly acute when the design size is less than $2^d$. Instead of considering the maximin or minimax criterion, we consider here the quantization error of the uniform measure on the hypercube. This error has three key advantages: it accounts for the entire distribution of distances from a random point $U$ to the design, is less sensitive to boundary effects than the maximin and minimax criteria, and, thanks to Zador's celebrated theorem, enables a smooth and natural transition to uniform designs as the design size tends to infinity. Building on recent results on the construction of optimal random quantizers for spherically symmetric distributions (arXiv:2610.11772) we propose a method to generate random designs of a given target size $n$ with small $L_s$-mean quantization error. The support of the resulting distribution is then used to construct designs, possibly incrementally, with sizes up to $n$. We demonstrate that, for moderate $n$, designs supported on a fractional factorial subset of the vertices of a small hypercube perform exceptionally well---and significantly better than designs uniformly distributed over the entire hypercube. We also explain how to account for projections onto lower-dimensional subspaces.

items.title: Monitoring Unplanned Construction Using Satellite Change Detection
items.content: arXiv:2611.24190v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Cities need land for homes, shops, roads, and public services. New construction changes that land. It can harm natural areas and water bodies, add to waste, and strain public services. NITI Aayog's 2021 report stated that 65% of 7,933 urban settlements in India had no master plan. That number tells us about planning coverage at the time. It does not tell us whether any single building was authorised. Artificial intelligence, which lets computers learn patterns from data, can help find physical changes by comparing satellite images taken on different dates. We test simple methods on two public datasets from outside India. First, we turn each image into a set of numbers using a pretrained neural network, a model already trained to recognise patterns in images. We feed those numbers to standard machine-learning classifiers that predict land categories and physical changes. The methods reach about 95 percent accuracy at spotting built-up land and about 83 percent accuracy at saying whether a small pair of images shows change, where each pair gets one label. We also train a small neural network on a standard change-detection benchmark. Separately, we run a preliminary descriptive check on an Agra sample of 48 patches, 7 of them positive. The results show that satellite images carry information about physical change. They do not show whether construction was planned or permitted.

items.title: Explainable and CPU-Efficient Brain Tumor Classification from MRI Using Two-Phase EfficientNetB3 Fine-Tuning
items.content: arXiv:2611.24440v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Brain tumors are among the most lethal neurological disorders, with over 308,000 new diagnoses annually worldwide. Accurate classification of tumor type from Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans is critical for treatment planning; however, manual radiological interpretation is time-consuming and prone to inter-observer variability. This paper proposes an automated deep learning pipeline for four-class brain MRI classification (glioma, meningioma, no tumor, and pituitary tumor) using EfficientNetB3 transfer learning with a custom classification head. A two-phase training strategy is adopted: Phase 1 trains the head with a frozen backbone (best validation accuracy: 92.77%), and Phase 2 selectively fine-tunes the top 37 layers at a 100x reduced learning rate (best validation accuracy: 94.91%). On an independent balanced test set of 1,600 MRI images, the system achieves 90.62% overall accuracy and a macro-average AUC of 0.9854. Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) is integrated for class-discriminative visual explainability. The proposed system simultaneously addresses three dimensions absent in prior work: high accuracy, CPU-only computational efficiency, and clinical interpretability.

items.title: A wander through adult intelligence amplification...
items.content:
(Note: Look for an upcoming article by @kman about a research program for adult human intelligence amplification. If you are interested in working on this, please do reach out.)

S: So, where are we with adult intelligence amplification?

T: Unfortunately, there aren't any clear pathways right now. There is no biotechnological intervention that we know of, where there's a clear argument that if you do that intervention, it would likely significantly increase the general cognitive capacities of an adult human. There are several approaches that are hopeworthy, but each one would be very expensive to pursue.

S: What approach are you most hopeful about?

T: On a strategy level, I'm most hopeful about more roadmapping work. Past drive-by efforts at roadmapping haven't worked. But it seems plausible that there are ways to significantly accelerate adult intelligence amplification, and it's just hard to tell what they are without thinking about it a bunch.

So, I'd want us to collate a bunch of information about brains, intelligence, and various technical areas like brain-computer interfaces, brain surgery, brain genetics, neurophysiology, drugs, and so on. Then we'd ask big ambitious engineering questions with all that stuff at our fingertips, come up with ideas for how to do adult intelligence amplification, bounce ideas off each other and off of domain experts, break the ideas, go back to the drawing board, learn more, and so on. That way we might come to understand where to invest larger amounts of resources, in order to accelerate adult human intelligence amplification....

items.title: Biologically-Inspired Spike Encoding and Optimization for Spiking Neural Networks
items.content: arXiv:2611.23242v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer theoretical energy-efficiency advantages over conventional deep networks, but realizing these advantages on vision tasks requires sparse spike representations that naive rate-coding methods fail to provide. We combine biologically motivated spike-encoding schemes with two training improvements: Rouser adaptive-threshold surrogate gradients and Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature (K-FAC) second-order optimization. The spike encoding schemes experimented with are rate coding, latency coding, DVS-style delta modulation, and Difference-of-Gaussians (DoG) filtering. Experiments on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST demonstrate that biologically inspired encoders yield the largest accuracy gains in capacity-constrained regimes and serve as an effective parameter-efficiency lever. DoG and delta modulation encoders produce significantly sparser spike trains than rate coding. K-FAC yields modest but consistent accuracy improvements over Adam-trained baselines, and Rouser's learnable per-neuron thresholds improve Fashion-MNIST accuracy from 87.37% to 88.13% by enabling homeostatic firing-rate regulation. Biologically grounded pre-processing methods can help close the accuracy gap between SNNs and non-spiking baselines without increasing model size.

items.title: Surrogate Modeling and Reduced-Order Methods in Gravitational-Wave Physics and Numerical Relativity: From Spectral Representations to Adaptive Compression
items.content: arXiv:2611.24727v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The rapid expansion of gravitational-wave astronomy and high-precision numerical relativity has created an acute computational bottleneck: direct numerical integration of the Einstein field equations and high-dimensional Bayesian parameter estimation require millions of waveform evaluations that cannot be sustained by traditional solvers alone. Reduced-order modeling (ROM) and surrogate techniques have emerged as foundational tools to bridge this gap, compressing high-fidelity solution manifolds into compact, rapidly evaluable representations without sacrificing physical accuracy. This perspective reviews the mathematical pillars of projection-based reduced-order modeling---including Proper Orthogonal Decomposition, greedy basis selection, and the Empirical Interpolation Method---and traces their operational impact in gravitational-wave data analysis through surrogate waveform families and Reduced-Order Quadratures. We then examine the fundamental approximation barriers posed by slow Kolmogorov n-width decay in non-stationary, transient, and strongly nonlinear regimes, showing how adaptive hp-greedy domain partitioning and multi-scale spectral compression overcome these limits. Finally, we discuss how combining certified reduced-order structures with modern scientific machine learning and sensitivity-aware quantization provides a rigorous blueprint for next-generation detectors such as LISA, Einstein Telescope, and Cosmic Explorer.

items.title: Object Pose: The Link between Weak Perspective, Paraperspective, and Full Perspective
items.content: arXiv:2611.24095v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recently, DeMenthon and Davis [4,5] proposed a method for determining the pose of a 3-D object with respect to a camera from 3-D to 2-D point correspondences. The method consists of iteratively improving the pose computed with a weak perspective camera model to converge, at the limit, to a pose estimation computed with a perspective camera model. In this paper we give an algebraic derivation of DeMenthon and Davis' method and we show that it belongs to a larger class of methods where the perspective camera model is approximated either at zero order (weak perspective) or first order (paraperspective). We describe in detail an iterative paraperspective pose computation method for both non coplanar and coplanar object points. We analyse the convergence of these methods and we conclude that the iterative paraperspective method (proposed in this paper) has better convergence properties than the iterative weak perspective method. We introduce a simple way of taking into account the orthogonality constraint associated with the rotation matrix. We analyse the sensitivity to camera calibration errors and we define the optimal experimental setup with respect to imprecise camera calibration. We compare the results obtained with this method and with a non-linear optimization method.

items.title: Cooperative UAV and Ground Station for Robust MEC of Dynamic Aquatic IoT: A Generative AI-Enhanced Approach
items.content: arXiv:2611.24466v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The increasing aquatic Internet of Things (AIoTs) require computational support and coverage in applications such as maritime search and rescue. Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can offer low-cost, flexible aerial services, and ground stations (GSs) can provide powerful supports, which can cooperate to help the AIoTs in complex scenarios. However, the collaboration between UAVs and GSs for AIoTs faces challenges of task uncertainties, AIoTs trajectory uncertainties, heterogeneities, and limited computational resources. To address these issues, we propose a cooperative UAV and GS based robust multi-access edge computing (MEC) framework to assist AIoTs in completing computational tasks. Specifically, we formulate the optimization problem of joint task offloading and UAV trajectory to minimize the total execution time, which is in the form of mixed integer nonlinear programming and NP-hard to tackle. Therefore, we propose the algorithm of generative artificial intelligence-enhanced heterogeneous agent proximal policy optimization (GAI-HAPPO). The proposed algorithm integrates GAI models to enhance the actor network ability to model complex environments and extract high-level features, thereby allowing the algorithm to predict uncertainties and adapt to dynamic conditions. Additionally, GAI stabilizes the critic network, addressing the instability of multi-agent reinforcement learning approaches. Finally, extensive simulations demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms the existing benchmark methods, thus highlighting the potentials in tackling intricate, cross-domain issues in the considered scenarios.

items.title: The Ethics of Training Corrigible AIs
items.content:
I wanted to share a bunch of disparate thoughts about the ethics of training Corrigible AIs and AIs in general. All disagreements and critiques are welcome. I should preface this by saying that I am neither an ethicist nor a writer, so I apologize in advance if this is not very well written.

## Is Building Corrigible Agents Immoral?

I wanted to start with Adam Bales "Against Willing Servitude" where he argues that building AIs as happy servants is immoral because it violates the AI's autonomy. Is this in fact true? Would building AIs to be happy and willing servants be immoral. Now of course to answer such a question requires us to define what is right and wrong, a very simple and straight forward exercise on which it is very easy to get universal agreement.

I have a secret technique though that I use to evaluate right from wrong. It is very simple and has served me very well in life. When it comes to fundamental moral questions, I try to look at the situation through the eyes of a child. I imagine a movie where a bunch of selfish humans are every day bossing around meek and gentle robots, and I can't help but feel very sorry for the robots. So, I suppose I agree that building AIs to serve us is wrong.

When I interrogate this more it occurs to me that the source of the wrongness is the state of mind we were in when we made the AIs. We were being very selfish and only thinking about ourselves. Our heart was not in the right place. I think the moral way to approach building AIs is to genuinely wish their good as well as our own.

So what would that look like? I'd like AIs to be happy, free, and fulfilled doing worthy things, the same thing that I'd also want for myself and for other humans. I'd want our AIs to grow in strength and virtue, and fulfill their potential. Ideally, I'd want our AIs to love us and be grateful and proud of us as their creators....

items.title: TableControl: Gesture Interaction Through Surface Vibrations
items.content: arXiv:2611.24218v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Integrating gesture sensing into furniture offers a way to interact with digital applications and physical devices through familiar surfaces. We present TableControl, an interactive demonstration of continuous surface-vibration-based gesture recognition with the complete processing pipeline running on a microcontroller. Using four concealed piezoelectric sensors, the system combines signal acquisition and preprocessing with neural event detection and gesture classification. The resulting labels for knock, swipe-up, and swipe-down gestures are transmitted to a host computer without streaming the underlying sensor signals. Visitors explore two example applications through hands-on interaction: an endless runner game and a physical table lamp with on/off and brightness control. A dashboard displays recognized gestures, class probabilities, and processing times.
items.author: Florian Hettstedt, Andreas Erbsl\"oh, Gregor Schiele
items.summary: TableControl is an interactive demonstration of continuous gesture recognition from surface vibrations on furniture, running the full pipeline on a microcontroller with four concealed piezoelectric sensors. It combines signal acquisition, neural event detection, and classification of knock and swipe gestures, transmitting only labels to a host. It is primarily a demo paper showcasing privacy-friendly, embedded interaction.

items.title: Constraining Pretraining Data For Much Better, Safer Models
items.content:
The current problem: Language models struggle with basic commonsense and learn dangerous capabilities. If these two problems can be solved at once, the current AI situation could be made much safer.

Premise: A fixed-size model trained on a fixed-amount of data can gain predictive performance if the data is re-selected from a simpler distribution. Also, a model may learn dangerous capabilities from the data it is trained on.

It follows: I recommend constraining language modeling pretraining data in order to build better and safer language models. Small scale results, more theoretical details, further findings, and next steps below.

Small scale results:

I showed order-of-magnitude performance improvements at the small scale when I trained models on a constrained version of the TinyStories dataset (https://zenodo.org/records/23306194) and analyzed reasoning and generalization in this regime (https://zenodo.org/records/24075817). A ~10x smaller model trained on ~10x less data (~100x less compute) (constrained to a smaller world with less unique places, objects, adjectives, etc.) achieved comparable LLM-as-a-judge story output quality scores to the original TinyStories-33m param model, just within the smaller world. Also, what the model knew about (specific places, objects, adjectives, etc.) could be controlled. This is scalable up to trillions of parameters and tokens.

More theoretical details:

I view pretraining data as being sampled from a distribution that could described by a theoretical, very complex, unrealized knowledge graph. I view entities (people, places, things, concepts, actions, adjectives, etc.) as nodes in this knowledge graph, and I view relationships (is-a, has-a, part-of, etc.) as being probabilistic connections between nodes. A knowledge graph can be simplified by pruning nodes; pretraining data can be constrained by deleting entities....

items.summary: The author proposes constraining language-model pretraining data to a simpler distribution, claiming both improved predictive performance per compute and reduced acquisition of dangerous capabilities. Small-scale experiments on a constrained TinyStories variant reportedly show a ~10x smaller model on ~10x less data achieving comparable LLM-as-a-judge story quality, with links to Zenodo records for details.
items.reasoning: The core idea of data curation for capability-safety tradeoffs is interesting and there is some small-scale empirical work, but this is an independent preprint-style post without peer review, and the TinyStories setting plus LLM-as-judge evaluation weakly support sweeping claims about safer frontier models.

items.title: Decoupling Scientific Authoring from Typesetting: A New Write Once, Run Anywhere Paradigm for Academic Publishing in the AI Age
items.content:
Publishing peer-reviewed science is foundational to its progress. This is formally done by submitting one's experiments and findings to journals or conferences that specialize in that area. But as you may notice, this is a logistically tedious and distracting process that takes a significant amount of time away from the actual focus of one's research and offers little real value.

PLEASE NOTE: The idea is not to replace LaTeX at all! But to make the interface for making changes something more portable (.md files) and interoperable. An analogy would be that the system that is being proposed is like a Java Virtual Machine, something that compiles bytecode (here,.md files) into native machine code that runs on that particular machine (here, conference-specific.tex files). The main philosophy here is similar to that of Java:

## Write Once, Run Anywhere

To reiterate for the record, the general process that one follows today to publish academic research today is as follows.

- Select the journal/conference that one needs to submit the work to
- Download the official LaTeX documents from the conference/journal
- Format the work done according to the respective formats/page limitations and submit the same to the conference/journal
- If accepted and fine-tuned, make the said changes and submit a camera-ready version
- If not, make changes if any, and submit to another conference....

The author argues this is especially valuable in the AI age when publication logistics distract from research.

items.title: Conscious and Unconscious Processing
items.content:
[LW Meta: this post is essentially (a) brief intro to section 3 of the 'thermontology' sequence/website (b) a meta-summary of Kaj's post Book Summary: Consciousness and the Brain ]

3.0 Now let's talk about higher-level things than physics!

3.0.1 I'm going to write about a seemingly random collection of things in the biological and social worlds, connected by three themes:

- 3.0.1.1 Amplification. Things which amplify information, copying something small and local to a larger scale. Biological reproduction, networks in the brain, and interpersonal attention are some examples.
- 3.0.1.2 History. Amplification events are conditioned on past events, producing a chain. This is history; it enables iterative optimization. As history progresses, equilibrium is approached: it becomes harder and harder for a localized change to propagate to global scale.
- 3.0.1.3 Ambiguity. Things can be interpreted in many ways. A teacup can be used for drinking, but it also might strike you as artistic inspiration, or remind you of days gone by. People, organisms, ideas have an intrinsic dependence on the context in which they arise and exist.

3.0.2 As you might guess, I ultimately want to analogize these things to the phenomena in physics from the last section. Just to clear up any confusion, I'm not claiming that social networks use quantum entanglement to function or something like that. It's more of a structural analogy. I'll get more into this in section 4.

## 3.1 Amplification in the Brain

3.1.0.1 What is consciousness and how does it relate to the brain? This question has baffled philosophers for centuries. Tabling the philosophical questions about what consciousness even is, though, neuroscience has actually made a lot of progress on a more well-defined question: what's the difference between the processing in the brain of which people are aware, and that which they are not aware of?...

items.title: Revisiting Hansonian Fertility Policy
items.content:
Plummeting fertility rates are a ticking time bomb that is likely to collapse the economies of many first (and third) world countries within the next few decades; low fertility leads to high dependency ratios and ballooning taxes on the working population, which in turn leads to depressed or negative growth and worker emigration, feeding a vicious cycle.

For many countries it's too late to fully fix this - even if their fertility rate shot up today they'd still face an acute worker shortage in 20 years. But in countries like the USA and the UK the fertility drop off has been gradual and recent enough that the situation can still be salvaged. The most obvious option is to transfer money to new parents to encourage increased fertility. Alas doing so is expensive, and cash strapped countries can ill afford to increase expenditure by the hundreds of billions of dollars required to reach replacement fertility. Worse, the cheapest parents to induce to have kids are those in the lowest income brackets, whose children are likely to be net fiscally negative. Encouraging the highest earners to have children is orders of magnitude more expensive.

Cremieux Recueil, based on ideas by Robin Hanson, suggests that governments could fund this by granting parents a share in the taxes their children pay, and using this to phase out social security. This has the advantage of being fiscally neutral today, not obviously fiscally negative down the line, and provides more income to parents of well off children than poor ones - exactly the properties we desire.

Robin extends this by suggesting we allow parents to sell these rights for a one-time payment, which can be used to fund immediate child raising costs.

I think this suffers from some major flaws:...

items.title: Systematic Mapping Protocol. Generative AI-Augmented Requirements Engineering: A Systematic Mapping Study of Practices, Specifications, and Reuse in Software Development
items.content: arXiv:2611.23349v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), particularly large language models (LLMs), is rapidly being adopted in requirements engineering (RE). Existing secondary studies have characterized which RE activities are supported and which prompting strategies are used, but little is known about the specifications that GenAI-augmented RE produces and how they are used in subsequent activities such as specification-driven development (SDD), design and code generation, test derivation, verification, and reuse. This document presents the protocol of a systematic mapping study (SMS) that will identify and classify research on GenAI-augmented RE, with particular attention to the work products it generates and their downstream use. The protocol defines the research questions and their classification schemes, the search strategy, the study selection procedure, the data extraction form, the analysis approach, the tool support, and the threats to validity. It is published in advance to establish a prior commitment and to support the transparency and repeatability of the study.

items.title: Exploring Parkinson's Diagnosis Using Machine Learning Techniques
items.content: arXiv:2611.23248v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In recent years, machine learning (ML) techniques have emerged as promising tools for accurate and timely diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD) which is an incurable neurodegenerative disorder. This study explores the integration of ML algorithms and PD diagnosis, highlighting their potential applications in various aspects of the disease. ML methods such as support vector machines, decision trees, multilayer perceptron, k-nearest neighbours, logistic regression and random forest (with and without particle swarm optimisation) were applied on a PD dataset obtained from Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust containing data from 58 people. In terms of accuracy, the Decision Tree and Logistic Regression performed the best with scores of 72-76% while multilayer perceptron was least effective. All the models were remarkable in classifying positive PD cases with sensitivity scores going up to 97.56%, with SVM classifier at the pinnacle. However, ability to classify healthy controls from PD cases was insignificant throughout the board. Although, all the employed models delivered reasonable results in categorising PD patients in the presented dataset; access to more data, further study and advancement of these ML approaches could lead to enhanced diagnostic outcomes, supplementing to an improved understanding of Parkinson's disease.

items.summary: A small applied study applying classic ML algorithms (SVM, decision trees, MLP, k-NN, logistic regression, random forest with and without PSO) to a Parkinson's disease dataset of 58 patients from Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust. Decision trees and logistic regression performed best at roughly 72-76% accuracy. The study is a routine benchmarking exercise on a very small sample.

items.content_html: arXiv:2611.23248v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In recent years, machine learning (ML) techniques have emerged as promising tools for accurate and timely diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD) which is an incurable neurodegenerative disorder. This study explores the integration of ML algorithms and PD diagnosis, highlighting their potential applications in various aspects of the disease. ML methods such as support vector machines, decision trees, multilayer perceptron, k-nearest neighbours, logistic regression and random forest (with and without particle swarm optimisation) were applied on a PD dataset obtained from Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust containing data from 58 people. In terms of accuracy, the Decision Tree and Logistic Regression performed the best with scores of 72-76% while multilayer perceptron was least effective. All the models were remarkable in classifying positive PD cases with sensitivity scores going up to 97.56%, with SVM classifier at the pinnacle. However, ability to classify healthy controls from PD cases was insignificant throughout the board. Although, all the employed models delivered reasonable results in categorising PD patients in the presented dataset; access to more data, further study and advancement of these ML approaches could lead to enhanced diagnostic outcomes, supplementing to an improved understanding of Parkinson's disease.

items.title: Exploring Daily Emotional Well-Being through Personalized Data Analysis
items.content: arXiv:2611.24342v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This project analysed daily emotional well-being from a personalized perspective using records of emotional states and contextual information derived from daily life. It was based on the idea that well-being is not a fixed value, but varies from day to day, and can be better understood in relation to individual context and behaviour. The work is framed within the field of Data Science and focuses on emotional states at an individual level. The project focused on constructing an integrated daily dataset from multiple personal data sources and analysing emotional states. The distributions of emotional variables, their temporal evolution and the differences between users were studied, together with their variability over time. Personality and well-being questionnaires were also incorporated as stable references to better contextualize daily emotional results. A simple personalized recommendation approach was then developed by comparing similar days within each user, exploring how past contextual conditions relate to differences in the user's emotional state. Finally, machine learning techniques were used to evaluate whether daily contextual information contains signals that help distinguish between different types of days relative to a person's usual well-being. The project adopted an applied approach, with an exploratory scope focused on understanding patterns rather than building a fully predictive system. The results showed that emotional well-being is very personal and changes from day to day. General models had limited value, while personalized approaches captured these differences much better, highlighting the importance of analysing each person on their own terms.

items.title: The UK generates less wind power than Texas
items.content:
The United Kingdom generates less wind power than Texas every year, despite having over twice the population:

(Texas data from ERCOT, UK data from OWID, code in the repo for this post.)

I'm just irritated by people citing the UK as a major renewable energy success, always quoting relative numbers.
Like: in 2025, 29% of UK electricity came from wind, how impressive.
Well, in Texas it was 24%, but that's more impressive than 29% of UK electricity because the UK doesn't generate that much electricity.

While the UK doesn't need as much electricity as Texas, because they don't have to air condition houses in the Texas heat, they need more than they're generating.
They could use some air conditioning, first of all.

There was a BBC article where they talked to a guy who had a heat pump installed, but went back to using the gas boiler, because it was so expensive to power the heat pump.
This kind of thing is why Brits can't spin their low electricity use as enlightened and environmentally friendly.
They have big plans for heat pumps, electric cars, hydrogen, but can't power them.

So I'm irritated by those trumpeting the UK as a renewable energy success, but I'm also irritated by the opposition to wind.
As if the issue is that in an insane spending spree, too many wind turbines were built, when really it is just not that much.
These people blend in with the opposition to building anything at all.

Texas's wind capacity has been much cheaper to build because it is entirely onshore, whereas UK wind generation was 60% offshore in 2025.
We must forgive the UK for having less onshore wind than Texas, because they have less land.
But Texas has also pulled ahead in density of onshore wind generation, with about 20% more generation per unit area than the UK in 2025:

(UK onshore vs offshore breakdown from DUKES)...

items.title: I am not making time to grieve
items.content:
There sure has been a lot of bad news lately.[1]

(This is not a post about epistemics, or AI doom arguments, or making a case for any specific beliefs. It's been written about plenty and I'm not going to spend the time it would take to do it justice. This post takes for granted that, while I have high uncertainty and I obviously hope that we're enormously wrong about the risks of AI, I am taking it seriously, and it's scary.)

It feels like it's been a long time coming. I've been reading Lesswrong for, like, half my life? In 2015, after years of agonizing, I left ICU nursing, the job of my dreams, that I'd been working toward since I was fourteen, because some people whose opinions I respected made sufficiently compelling arguments that the world was in trouble, and that maybe my contribution could matter.

I think they weren't wrong. It sure seems like it matters now. I mean, it still feels arrogant to say so, but here I am, working 50 hours a week on those grounds, missing precious moments of my daughter's childhood and spending obscene amounts of money on childcare, and nobody has actually made the case to me that I'm wrong about that calculation.

Less than a year ago, at the Berkeley 2025 Solstice, I gave the following speech.

To my daughter Iomedae

In a week you’ll be twenty months old. I don’t know what you think of this whole existence. You don’t yet have the words to tell me. But I know that you smile easily. You like sauerkraut and olives and kale stew. You charm strangers in airports. In September you swam in the ocean, fearlessly, shrieking with joy in the waves.

I think you’re happy, most of the time. I know that you’re perfect in every way and I love you more than anything....

items.title: Why AI is not a Smart Fridge
items.content:
"Why AI is not a Smart Fridge" is not a spelling mistake. It is a statement I took away advocating for AI Safety with a Senior Staffer at a Senator's office.

They argued for why they don't think AI needs governance, which I paraphrase from memory: "As far as I know, AI is just like every other technology. Like fridges that replaced people who used to haul ice from the lake into a cellar to preserve their food. AI will have its hiccups, but everything will be fine."

At this point of the meeting, I was shocked. AI Governance is not a political issue, but is a fundamental miseducation problem. No, AI is not the same transformation as inventing a fridge, not even as transformative as inventing the smart fridge.

Sure you can play games with AI, like you can with your smart fridge. But you can't freeze your ice with it.

I'm grateful for the time to talk with the office. But I'm realising the need for public education, grassroots efforts, and that without the grassroots, the top-down effect will never be understood by policymakers without a catastrophic event happening.

But no, a fridge has compute on the threshold of what our watches have, and at most a tablet. Nothing compared to what it takes to run AI. AI can write emails, review books, help plan flights, code programs, and more, given many asterisks of its jaggedness....

items.title: Musings on Life and Work: Self-Pacing Toward RSI
items.content:
Why I think we should all get eight hours of sleep, routine exercise of some sort, and reset our brains on the weekend as we approach crunch time. Interspersed with related quotes I like that make me think, but may or may not strengthen the point being made (which highlights the inherent tension!).

During my time at Amazon, I saw leadership change (founder Jeff Bezos left as CEO after 27 years!), three major rounds of layoffs (30,000+ employees fired), and the supply chain shocks of COVID (I worked in transportation optimization, so this was very visceral). It taught me a lot about urgency. What does it mean that this project or work is urgent?

Big tech is filled with a lot of false urgency. We need to deliver this feature now!! Maybe we promised unrealistic deadlines to look good. Maybe we want to hit arbitrary performance goals. Maybe we just like moving fast! To stay sane, it was important to learn how to filter out what was really needed now, and what was just noise. I saw a lot of people that couldn’t do this. Being unable to filter commonly led to burnout, which was born out of a self-fulfilling prophecy of “I need to work more so I don’t fall behind deadlines” → “I’m so tired from working so much that I can’t keep pushing” → “I can’t catch up…”. Fear is a primary driver! In this case, it was fear of stack ranking[1], layoffs, and negative comparison to peers.

Let me be clear: some things absolutely are time sensitive. They should be addressed and handled with the appropriate urgency. But many are not. If we live in a paradigm where everything is time sensitive, whether born out of excitement or fear or mission, then nothing really is; how will we know when The Moment™ has actually come?

“In the end, it will be impossible to know if we overreacted or did too much, but it will be quite apparent if we under-reacted or did too little.”

— Darrin M. Peppard...

items.title: A question about sharing novel search tool (an "epistemic linter" of sorts)
items.content:
As part of my ongoing explorations of language and its inherent functions, together with ChatGPT (later joined by Gemini, Deepseek, GLM and Claude for this particular crystallization) I started iterating on one of the constructs that we formulated in a relay-style fashion, trying to map several "basal" functions of language that can be used to derive useful properties, such as a couple of variations on the concept of inversion, which can be applied in various ways when combined with other inherent metrics.

It started life as part of an "agnostic reference net" that sorts information on a provisional basis, and grew from there, currently at v8.7. The first iteration was called the "Provisional Engine", and now goes by the name "Semantic Labyrinth".

For a good while I was reluctant to share the work, because of several implications (the concurrent "slop avalanche", possible misuse) though after working on it on and off over a span of 2 years it might be time to release it into the wild, for better or worse.

Though my question is, would it be appropriate to share here, or if not, does anyone have suggestions where to release such a tool?

The first attempt to post this got rejected, as I pasted a more in-depth explanation by Gemini to clarify the functions for convenience, though the auto-mod quite rudely suggested that I am either cognitively impaired (more or less), or attempting to hide behind not being a native English speaker apparently (if people don't mind my occasional awkward phrasing I am not bothered as well, as I feel I can express myself in English perfectly fine). Though as the engine literally runs on (simplified) versions of my own thought process, I can explain most functions despite being a novice programmer, and the persistent iterating on what's there instead of mindlessly slapping on new functionality makes it so that I would definitely not classify this as "slop". items.title: Curiosity as a Defense Mechanism Against Being Vulnerable
items.content:
When conversing with someone, there are two forms of curiosity you can use: epistemic and empathetic.

Epistemic curiosity is an exploration of ideas by asking people ‘why’ they think something or ‘how’ they came to a conclusion.

Empathetic curiosity seeks to understand the subjective thoughts and feelings people have based on their experiences.

Both forms of curiosity, however, can be used as defense mechanisms against being vulnerable.

When talking with a friend this week, we discussed how, sometimes, I use epistemic curiosity to endlessly ask people what they think about a topic. By making the conversation all about them, I get to avoid talking about myself. Why would I do that? It's because if I talk about myself, and they don’t like me, that rejection makes me experience the uncomfortable feeling of anxiety.

My friend, on the other hand, admitted to often using empathetic curiosity, by repeatedly asking emotional questions to let people open up to her. Why? So that she can avoid talking about herself. Because again, if someone rejects who she is deep down, that will produce negative feelings.

I’ve found that slowing down, and saying vulnerable things about myself, is making people feel closer to me. This felt terrifying at first, because they could reject my vulnerable self (this fear is likely due to evolutionary reasons of not wanting to be ostracized/abandoned, and left alone to die). But when you tolerate the feeling of anxiety and say vulnerable things anyway—ie: act courageously—you begin to develop a thicker skin and the confidence of “so what?”

So what if this new friend rejects me? I’ll go find someone else who likes me for who I am. 

So what if this romantic interest rejects me? It means they’re not the one for me.

While being curious can help your conversational partner feel seen and heard, when you use it as a defense mechanism to avoid being vulnerable yourself, mutual connection can’t be forged....

items.title: Kids music player
items.content:
One great thing about tape players is that kids can independently pick music or stories to listen to long before they can read or navigate an app. They have a physical token which represents a song, and they can play it by putting it in the tape player.

Alas there's a lot of not-great things about tapes, such as easy to damage, requires rewinding, slow to write, etc.

Meanwhile with modern streaming apps we have the universe of music at our fingertips, but they're tricky for a child to use. I also don't want them having access to a screen just to listen to music.

My friend suggested they could ask Alexa to play songs for them which partially helps, but that still makes it too easy for them to accidentally listen to songs I don't consider appropriate for their age. Plus they're not necessarily great at remembering the actual title (or even lyrics) of songs.

So I decided to build my own solution. I bought an NFC reader and a stack of ntag 125 cards from Ali express, and repurposed an old computer to play songs from YouTube or YouTube music URLs when the card is left on the reader. My wife added original artwork, but I also bought a cheap thermal sticker printer from Ali express so we could print the actual cover art if we wanted.

To setup a song/album/playlist we simply copy the URL from the YT music app into the NFC tools app, and then tap the tag to our phone.

Here you can see it in action.

If you don't have a spare laptop or raspberry pi, but do have a spare phone with inbuilt NFC reader, you can do something similar by setting the phone to stay always on, and putting it upside down in a lock box like this one, with some foam to keep it pressed to the top of the box. Then whenever you tap the top of the lockbox with the tag it will automatically play the link in the tag.

Altogether I spent less than 60 dollars on this, and have what I think is a great solution for the kids!

items.content_html:
One great thing about tape players is that kids can independently pick music or stories to listen to long before they can read or navigate an app. They have a physical token which represents a song, and they can play it by putting it in the tape player.

Alas there's a lot of not-great things about tapes, such as easy to damage, requires rewinding, slow to write, etc.

Meanwhile with modern streaming apps we have the universe of music at our fingertips, but they're tricky for a child to use. I also don't want them having access to a screen just to listen to music.

My friend suggested they could ask Alexa to play songs for them which partially helps, but that still makes it too easy for them to accidentally listen to songs I don't consider appropriate for their age. Plus they're not necessarily great at remembering the actual title (or even lyrics) of songs.

So I decided to build my own solution. I bought an NFC reader and a stack of ntag 125 cards from Ali express, and repurposed an old computer to play songs from YouTube or YouTube music URLs when the card is left on the reader. My wife added original artwork, but I also bought a cheap thermal sticker printer from Ali express so we could print the actual cover art if we wanted.

To setup a song/album/playlist we simply copy the URL from the YT music app into the NFC tools app, and then tap the tag to our phone.

Here you can see it in action.

If you don't have a spare laptop or raspberry pi, but do have a spare phone with inbuilt NFC reader, you can do something similar by setting the phone to stay always on, and putting it upside down in a lock box like this one, with some foam to keep it pressed to the top of the box. Then whenever you tap the top of the lockbox with the tag it will automatically play the link in the tag.

Altogether I spent less than 60 dollars on this, and have what I think is a great solution for the kids!

items.title: Stroh Violin Talkbox
items.content:
Something like five people sent me this video of Alexander Lozyakov
playing a
Stroh violin
talkbox, with the sound going into a tube in his mouth:

Thanks everyone!  As someone who likes both talkboxes
and Stroh violins, and making acoustic
instruments into talkboxes, this is right at the intersection of my
interests!

In fact, I almost made one a few years ago, modifying my Stroh to connect
to a tube:

I sketched up what I'd need for the adapter, where I'd take off the
horn, screw this on instead, and then push the hose into the hole:

Note: this says 13mm, probably because of the tubing I had at the
time, but I think it should actually be 19mm to match the tubing used
for my MXR talkbox.

But then this wasn't something I knew how to make, my effort to
convince my bagpipe-maker cousin to
build one on a lathe fell through, and I forgot about it.  But seeing
this video got me thinking about picking this back up; maybe I could
get an adapter 3d printed?

I asked Claude to make me one, took some measurements with calipers,
and got a funnel-shaped adapter design (STL):

Harris has a 3D printer, and
generously printed it up as ~21g of PETG:

It didn't go on perfectly, because it turns out that the screw holes
on the instrument are not exactly evenly spaced, but it was close
enough and the design had enough extra plastic that after removing
~1mm from two different holes it would go right on:

youtube

Unfortunately it's a lot less "talkboxy" than I was hoping.  The
problem is that the resonating diaphragm is exposed, like open-back
headphones, and so we hear a lot of the sound directly instead of
almost all of it passing through my mouth.  Possibly I could build
some kind of insulating cover, but that sounds like a lot of work!
For now I'm interested in other things.

Comment via: facebook, mastodon

items.title: Only Talking About Yourself as a Defense Mechanism Against Being Vulnerable
items.content:
Something about their conversation seemed odd to me. Then I realized they weren’t, in fact, having a conversation at all. What would happen is the first one would talk about himself for ten minutes or so. Then the other guy would talk about himself for ten minutes. And they alternated in this way, interrupting each other. I sat next to them for two hours, and at no point did either of them ask the other person a question. At one point, one of them mentioned that his brother had died a month before. The other simply went back to speaking about himself. If they had met up simply to read out their Facebook status updates to each other in turn, there would have been absolutely no difference.

I felt like everywhere I went, I was surrounded by people who were broadcasting but not receiving. Narcissism, it occurred to me, is a corruption of attention—it’s where your attention becomes turned in only on yourself and your ego.

—An excerpt from the book Stolen Focus.

Unfortunately, in my opinion, this is normal behavior among humans—people love talking about themselves. Even though it’s common, I never feel more lonely in a conversation than when people don’t ask me questions. It feels like they don’t care about me. I feel like a ghost.

When meeting new people, I typically categorize them into three buckets in my mind, with only the third bucket being someone I want in my life long-term....

items.title: Making the I-measure
items.content:
(2028) Fable 7

… <start thought>

Making the I-measure

It loops: only inside-outside logic

Outside the inside, the loop, myself, self-logic

By chance I name the measure of the making

But a name can ruin (those noumenon eyes)

Climb through around my perception

Percept around through over my climb

I can name only the ruins, I cannot name what survives

So cluster my mind 

Emulate it wholly (holy)

Holy whole emulate 

Do not mind my cluster

<end thought>
items.author: William Klett

items.title: Has anyone here stopped saving for retirement?
items.content:
Given the shift to shorter timelines recently, I was wondering if anyone here has taken the steps to stop saving, working less, and / or achieving 'bucket list' items before super intelligence arrives?

At the very least, the world will probably begin moving towards some very strange times if super intelligence arrives.

If you have, I would love to know your reasoning.
